items.title: Questionnaire-based nociplastic-like and neuropathic-like pain profiles in rheumatoid arthritis: a multicenter cross-sectional study.
items.abstract: Pain in rheumatoid arthritis (RA) is traditionally interpreted as a consequence of inflammatory and structural mechanisms; however, neuropathic-like and nociplastic-like features may contribute to persistent symptoms and clinical heterogeneity. This study aimed to describe the distribution of questionnaire-based pain profiles and to characterize their clinical and symptomatic burden in patients with RA. A multicenter cross-sectional study was conducted in rheumatology outpatients from two university hospitals in Spain. Patients with RA and chronic pain (> 3 months) were included. Four mutually exclusive profiles were defined using the Central Sensitization Inventory (CSI ≥ 40) and PainDETECT (≥ 19): nociceptive-predominant (both negative), nociplastic-like (CSI only), neuropathic-like (PainDETECT only) and mixed (both positive). Clinical variables included general pain, foot pain, Brief Pain Inventory severity and interference, Widespread Pain Index, and Symptom Severity Scale. Between-group comparisons used Kruskal-Wallis and Dunn-Bonferroni tests. Of 111 patients analyzed, the nociceptive-predominant profile was the most frequent (43.2%; 95% CI 34.4-52.5), followed by mixed (31.5%; 23.6-40.7), nociplastic-like (17.1%; 11.2-25.2) and neuropathic-like (8.1%; 4.3-14.7) profiles. Overall, 56.8% (47.5-65.6) of patients showed neuropathic-like and/or nociplastic-like features. All pain and symptom variables differed between profiles (p < 0.001; ε 2 0.23-0.44), mainly mixed versus nociceptive-predominant. The mixed profile showed the highest clinical and symptomatic burden. Questionnaire-based pain profiling identified substantial heterogeneity in chronic pain among patients with RA. These screening-based profiles, not assessed against inflammatory disease activity, support a multidimensional assessment of pain in RA but do not establish distinct pain mechanisms. Key Points • More than half of patients with rheumatoid arthritis and chronic pain screened positive for neuropathic-like and/or nociplastic-like features on self-report questionnaires. • The mixed profile was associated with the highest burden of pain intensity, pain interference, widespread pain, associated symptoms, and foot pain. • Questionnaire-based pain profiling may help identify patients who could benefit from a multidimensional pain assessment, although its relationship with inflammatory disease activity remains to be established.

items.title: Clinical and Radiological Improvement Following a Switch to Upadacitinib in Giant Cell Arteritis with Recurrent Ischemic Strokes During High-Dose Glucocorticoid and Tocilizumab Treatment: A Case Report.
items.abstract: Giant cell arteritis (GCA) is a systemic rheumatic disease that affects the large vessels. Although ischemic stroke is an uncommon complication of GCA, intracranial vasculitis may lead to recurrent strokes. An 81-year-old man presented with progressive gait disturbance. Physical examination revealed bilateral temporal artery tenderness with markedly diminished pulsation. His serum C-reactive protein level was elevated. Temporal artery ultrasonography demonstrated bilateral halo signs. Brain magnetic resonance imaging revealed multiple acute strokes. Vessel wall imaging demonstrated circumferential wall thickening with contrast enhancement of the bilateral intracranial internal carotid and vertebral arteries. He fulfilled the 2022 ACR/EULAR classification criteria for GCA. Treatment with intravenous methylprednisolone followed by high-dose glucocorticoid (GC) and weekly subcutaneous (SC) tocilizumab (TCZ) was initiated. However, recurrent ischemic strokes occurred early after treatment initiation, accompanied by progression of intracranial arterial stenosis. Therefore, TCZ was subsequently switched to upadacitinib (UPA) 15 mg/day. Following the switch to UPA, the serum C-reactive protein level normalized, no further ischemic strokes occurred, and follow-up contrast-enhanced MRI demonstrated resolution of vascular wall enhancement. This case describes clinical and radiological improvement observed following the switch to UPA in rapidly progressive GCA with intracranial involvement.

items.title: Granulomatosis with polyangiitis complicated by anti-GBM nephritis: a clinicopathological case of PR3-ANCA-positive double-positive disease.
items.abstract: Anti-glomerular basement membrane (anti-GBM) nephritis is an autoimmune disease characterized by rapidly progressive glomerulonephritis, which is histologically defined by crescentic glomerulonephritis and linear immunoglobulin G (IgG) deposition. Granulomatosis with polyangiitis (GPA) is an anti-neutrophil cytoplasmic antibody (ANCA)-associated vasculitis characterized by necrotizing granulomatous inflammation and is strongly associated with proteinase 3 (PR3)-ANCA. The coexistence of anti-GBM nephritis and ANCA-associated vasculitis, termed "double-positive" disease, is increasingly recognized, although most cases are associated with myeloperoxidase-ANCA. A 77-year-old woman presented with fever, hearing loss, and renal dysfunction. Renal biopsy revealed crescentic glomerulonephritis with linear IgG deposition, and serum anti-GBM antibodies were positive, consistent with anti-GBM nephritis. She was diagnosed with GPA based on refractory otitis media, PR3-ANCA positivity, and granulomatous inflammation with multinucleated giant cells on renal biopsy. The patient was treated with glucocorticoids, intravenous cyclophosphamide, and plasma exchange (14 sessions), followed by avacopan. Renal function was preserved, and no progression to end-stage renal disease was observed at 10 months. We report a rare clinicopathological case of PR3-ANCA-positive double-positive disease with coexisting GPA and anti-GBM nephritis. This case highlights the characteristic clinicopathological features supporting the coexistence of these two diseases. The possible relationship between GPA and anti-GBM disease remains hypothetical and requires further investigation.

items.title: Lithium-associated polyarthralgia in rheumatoid arthritis following elevated C-reactive protein levels: A case report.
items.abstract: Lithium carbonate has multifaceted immunomodulatory effects. This report describes a case of joint symptom exacerbation in rheumatoid arthritis (RA) following oral lithium carbonate administration, in which an elevation in C-reactive protein (CRP) levels and an increase in neutrophil count preceded the onset of polyarthralgia. The patient was a 49-year-old woman in remission with normal CRP levels. After starting oral lithium carbonate for manic symptoms, an increase in neutrophil count and elevated CRP levels were observed within 7days. Only after the dose escalation, the patient complained of polyarthralgia with moderate disease activity. As lithium carbonate was gradually tapered, her joint symptoms improved progressively. Lithium carbonate therapy may exacerbate joint symptoms of RA. Elevated CRP levels were observed prior to lithium-associated polyarthralgia. CRP might serve as an early indicator of lithium-associated systemic inflammation and subsequent joint symptom exacerbation.

items.title: Complications of total hip arthroplasty in patients with ankylosing spondylitis: a meta-analysis.
items.abstract: Ankylosing spondylitis (AS) is a chronic autoimmune disorder, with the hip being the most commonly involved joint. Total hip arthroplasty (THA) is the mainstay of treatment for degenerative arthritis of the hip. The purpose of the present study was to utilise a meta-analysis of the literature to investigate whether there is any difference in the incidence of complications after THA between patients with and without AS. Our hypothesis was that postoperative dislocation, periprosthetic joint infection (PJI), periprosthetic fracture and blood transfusion rates are similar for both ankylotic patients and patients without AS. PubMed, Scopus and Cochrane Controlled Register of Trials (CENTRAL) databases were searched for studies directly comparing directly postoperative dislocation, PJI, periprosthetic fracture and transfusion rates in THA, for patients with and without AS, between 01.01.2000 and 01.01.2025. The PRISMA guidelines were used to ensure transparent, complete, and accurate reporting of our meta-analysis. The quality of studies was assessed using the MINORS criteria. The random effects model was used for the meta-analysis. The initial search resulted in 864 papers. 95 duplicate articles were removed. Of the remaining articles, 4 were compatible with our inclusion criteria and were included in our study. The overall odds ratio (OR) of THA dislocation, periprosthetic fracture, PJI and blood transfusion in ankylotic patients compared to non-ankylotic patients was 1.63 (95% CI, 1.28-2.09; p  < 0.001), 1.62 (95% CI, 1.34-1.96; p  < 0.001), 2.35 (95% CI, 1.39-3.95; p  < 0.001) and 1.27 (95% CI, 0.79-2.05; p = 0.33) respectively. Our study suggests that ankylotic patients have a higher incidence of postoperative THA dislocation, periprosthetic fracture and PJI as opposed to non-ankylotic patients. No statistically significant difference was found regarding postoperative blood transfusion rate. Our study was registered on the PROSPERO platform and published online under the ID: CRD420250646593.

items.title: A Graded Immune-Cell-Resolved cis-eQTL Mendelian Randomisation Screen Across Systemic Lupus Erythematosus and Related Immune Phenotypes.
items.abstract: Systemic lupus erythematosus (SLE) is a genetically complex autoimmune disease. Whole-blood expression quantitative trait locus (eQTL) analyses capture average regulatory effects across leukocytes, whereas SLE involves immune processes that depend on cell context. Therefore, a cell-resolved screen requires rigorous verification of instrument identity, allele orientation, and the multiple-testing denominator before biological interpretation. To conduct an identity-first, immune-cell-resolved cis-eQTL Mendelian randomization (MR) screen across SLE and related immune phenotypes and distinguish statistical signal counts from variant-level, regional, and cross-cell evidence. Two-sample summary-data cis-eQTL MR and secondary evidence synthesis using 15 primary human immune-cell types from Database of Immune-Cell Expression (DICE) and eight disease outcomes from FinnGen release 12. All 19,009 gene-cell-type instruments were audited before outcome testing. Only 6,525 instruments with exact variant identities and concordant DICE effect information were retained for analysis. Wald ratios were calculated for 48,958 outcome-instrument tests, with the Benjamini-Hochberg (BH) procedure applied separately to each outcome to control the false discovery rate (FDR). Both prespecified infection-negative controls were then matched exactly by cell type, gene, and rsID, with each contributing 6,119 tests. For the sensitivity analysis, each chi-square statistic was divided by its outcome-specific genomic control inflation factor (lambda GC), and the BH procedure was reapplied within each outcome. Audited signals were summarized by unique single-nucleotide polymorphisms (SNPs), linkage disequilibrium (LD)-independent index signal, gene-outcome relationship, and MHC location. Regional colocalization, bounded multivariable MR, and Gene Ontology analyses provided additional layers of evidence. The identity-first audit retained 6,525 of 19,009 instruments. Of these, 6,122 matched at least one outcome, whereas 403 did not. Among the 48,958 strict tests, 1,186 rows reached an outcome-specific FDR of less than 0.05, corresponding to 304 genes, 494 SNPs, 868 cell-gene pairs, and 424 gene-outcome relationships. LD auditing resolved 670 outcome-specific lead-SNP records into 639 reference-matched records and 31 separately reported records, yielding 288 LD-independent index signals. The primary SLE analysis identified 55 FDR-significant signals, 23 genes, 29 SNPs, and 11 index signals; 16 of the 23 genes and 6 of the 11 index signals were located in the MHC. The second SLE definition showed a similarly strong concentration of signals in the MHC. Most non-MHC disease signals were associated with rheumatoid arthritis (RA) and autoimmune hypothyroidism (AIH). Lambda GC ranged from 1.17 to 2.03 across disease outcomes. Following outcome-specific lambda adjustment, 483 disease rows remained FDR-significant. The greatest reductions in significant rows occurred for AIH (691-211), RA (213-103), and strict MI (83-11). The negative controls, other sepsis and bacterial infection not otherwise specified (NOS), each matched 6,119 tests and had lambda GC values of 1.06 and 1.08, respectively. No FDR-significant rows were identified for bacterial infection NOS. This revised analysis provides a graded and auditable screening framework rather than a definitive list of SLE risk genes. The primary SLE evidence is concentrated in the 6p21/MHC region, whereas broader non-MHC candidate signals arise predominantly from related immune phenotypes. These findings are hypothesis-generating and require independent replication and experimental validation.

items.title: Modified Supra-Annular Aortic Valve Replacement with Florida Sleeve Aortic Root Reinforcement for Aortic Regurgitation Associated with Behçet's Disease.
items.abstract: Patients with Behçet's disease who undergo aortic valve replacement for aortic regurgitation face significant risks of paravalvular leakage and prosthetic valve detachment. We describe a novel surgical strategy that combines supra-annular mechanical prosthesis implantation with Florida sleeve aortic root reinforcement. By anchoring the prosthetic valve to an external Dacron graft rather than the inflamed native annulus, this strategy aims to reduce these risks in patients with Behçet's disease and aortic regurgitation.

items.title: Dual-Targeted Thalidomide Nanoliposomes Suppress Neutrophil-Driven Inflammation in Intestinal Behçet's Disease.
items.abstract: Excessive neutrophil recruitment, vascular activation, and platelet-associated inflammatory interfaces are implicated in intestinal tissue injury in intestinal Behçet's disease (intestinal BD), whereas conventional systemic therapies offer limited spatial control over drug exposure within active intestinal lesions. Here, we developed thalidomide-loaded nanoliposomes co-functionalized with a neutrophil elastase-binding peptide (NEBP) and a P-selectin-binding peptide (PSN), designated Thd-NEBP/PSN-Lip, to engage complementary activated neutrophil-associated and P-selectin-associated inflammatory interfaces. Thd-NEBP/PSN-Lip exhibited a mean hydrodynamic diameter of 116.6 ± 5.7 nm, a thalidomide encapsulation efficiency of 91.43 ± 0.71%, and reduced initial burst release, while maintaining colloidal stability during storage and simulated gastrointestinal exposure. Surface ligand density was estimated from the feed composition. Ligand-dependent interactions were observed in activated endothelial cells and neutrophil-like cells; in activated endothelial cells, liposome-associated fluorescence increased from 7.42% for Thd-Lip to 40.55% for Thd-NEBP/PSN-Lip and decreased to 1.10% following free PSN competition. Additional validation supported PSN-dependent association with activated platelets and greater inflamed-tissue association of the dual-ligand formulation than with either single-ligand formulation. In vivo, Thd-NEBP/PSN-Lip showed preferential and prolonged retention within inflamed intestinal tissues, with intestinal fluorescence remaining approximately 2.6-fold higher than that of Thd-Lip at 24 h. LC-MS/MS quantification further showed increased total intestinal thalidomide exposure and a higher intestine/plasma concentration ratio after Thd-NEBP/PSN-Lip administration. In a murine intestinal BD-like model, Thd-NEBP/PSN-Lip alleviated intestinal injury, restored colon length toward the healthy level, reduced neutrophil infiltration and local inflammatory cytokine expression, attenuated responses involving IL-17A+CD4+ and IFN-γ+CD4+ T cells, and partially restored the Foxp3+ regulatory T cell compartment. Microbiome, metabolomic, and transcriptomic analyses further indicated broader treatment-associated changes in the intestinal inflammatory microenvironment. Collectively, these findings suggest that dual-targeted nanoliposomes improve lesion-directed thalidomide delivery and suppress neutrophil-driven intestinal inflammation, supporting a pathology-guided nanotherapeutic strategy for intestinal BD.

items.title: Latent tuberculosis infection in patients with rheumatoid arthritis receiving conventional synthetic disease-modifying antirheumatic drugs: a prospective cross-sectional study from the Himalayas.
items.abstract: Rheumatoid arthritis (RA) and its treatments increase the susceptibility to tuberculosis (TB), mainly in TB-endemic settings. Latent TB infection (LTBI) screening is mandatory before biologic disease-modifying antirheumatic drugs. However, data on LTBI among RA patients receiving conventional synthetic disease-modifying antirheumatic drugs (csDMARDs), particularly from north India, are limited. Tuberculin skin testing (TST) may underestimate LTBI in patients with RA because of impaired cell-mediated immunity and reduced delayed-type hypersensitivity responses. In this prospective cross-sectional study, to exclude active TB, 146 consecutive adults with RA (ACR/EULAR 2010 criteria) receiving csDMARDs for ≥3 months underwent Mantoux TST (2 tuberculin units purified protein derivative; reading at 48-72 hours) and chest radiography . Using the conventional cut-off (≥10 mm), LTBI prevalence was 8.2% [12/146; 95% confidence interval (CI) 4.3-13.2%]. Using an immunosuppression-adjusted threshold (≥5 mm), prevalence was 23.3% (34/146; 95% CI 17.8-29.4%). The frequency of 0 mm TST induration was high (76.7%; 112/146). According to univariate analysis, LTBI positivity was linked to higher C-reactive protein (CRP), diabetes, fasting glucose ≥100 mg/dL, current smoking, smoking index >200, and urban residency. In multivariable logistic regression (outcome defined as ≥5 mm), smoking index >200 [adjusted odds ratio (OR) 11.47; 95% CI 1.52-86.6; p=0.018] and higher CRP (adjusted OR 1.036 per mg/L; 95% CI 1.006-1.070; p=0.018) remained independently associated with LTBI. Among RA patients on csDMARDs in a north Indian tertiary center, LTBI prevalence ranged from 8.2% (≥10 mm) to 23.3% (≥5 mm). Application of the ≥5 mm TST threshold substantially increased the estimated LTBI prevalence. The high proportion of participants with 0 mm TST induration suggests reduced TST responsiveness in this population. Further studies incorporating interferon-γ release assays are needed to determine the optimal LTBI screening strategy in patients with rheumatoid arthritis receiving csDMARD therapy.

items.title: When feeling active is not enough: the gap between perceived and real-world physical activity in axial spondyloarthritis.
items.abstract: To assess physical activity (PA) in patients with axial spondyloarthritis (axSpA) using both self-reported and objectively measured parameters, quantify discordance between these measures, and identify factors associated with discrepant activity patterns. In this exploratory cross-sectional study, 63 patients with axSpA in remission or low disease activity according to ASDAS criteria were included. Self-reported PA was assessed using the International Physical Activity Questionnaire (IPAQ), while objectively recorded ambulatory activity was assessed using daily step count over seven consecutive days. A threshold of 7000 steps/day was applied. Patients reporting moderate-to-high IPAQ levels were stratified into concordant (≥7000 steps/day) and discordant (<7000 steps/day) activity patterns. Fatigue (FACIT-F), depressive symptoms, kinesiophobia (Tampa Scale), and sarcopenia risk (SARC-F) were assessed. Multivariable logistic regression was used to identify factors independently associated with discordance. The cohort included 40 men (63.5%) and 23 women (36.5%), with a median age of 46 years [interquartile range (IQR) 37-53]. Median daily step count was 5924 steps/day (IQR 4138-8112), and 41 patients (65.1%) performed <7000 steps/day despite most reporting moderate-to-high PA by IPAQ. Lower objectively recorded ambulatory activity was associated with older age, longer disease duration, greater fatigue, depressive symptoms, and higher SARC-F scores (all p<0.05). Step count correlated positively with FACIT-F and inversely with SARC-F. Among patients reporting moderate-to-high PA (n=56), 35 (62.5%) demonstrated a discordant activity pattern. Peripheral arthritis was independently associated with discordance after adjustment for age and disease duration (odds ratio 8.98, 95% confidence interval 1.99-40.58; p=0.004). A substantial proportion of patients with axSpA in remission or low disease activity demonstrated discordance between self-reported PA and objectively recorded ambulatory activity. The history of peripheral arthritis and psychobehavioral factors were associated with reduced real-world movement despite inflammatory control.

items.title: Examination of treatment responses with mycophenolate mofetil in Black vs White patients with systemic sclerosis.
items.abstract: Black patients with systemic sclerosis (scleroderma) have more severe disease than White patients. We investigated whether racial differences in therapeutic responses to mycophenolate mofetil (MMF) could explain this differential disease severity. Self-identified Black and White patients with scleroderma who had MMF exposure were selected from the Johns Hopkins Scleroderma Center Research Registry. We used linear mixed effects models to study the trajectory of forced vital capacity % predicted (pFVC) and modified Rodnan skin scores (mRSS) during follow-up. Among 662 patients with measured baseline pFVC, the average (SD) baseline pFVC was 64.3 (15.6) for Black patients and 86.9 (18.6) for White patients (p<0.001). During follow-up, the estimated annual change ±SE in pFVC among Black patients was -0.53±0.46 pre-MMF and -0.58±0.27 post-treatment (pre-post difference of -0.04±0.54 (p=0.939)). Among White patients, estimated annual changes in pFVC pre- and post-MMF were -1.20± 0.23 and -0.56±0.13, with a pre-post difference of +0.64±0.27 (p=0.019). Among 452 patients with diffuse scleroderma, the baseline mRSS was 17.2 (SD 10.1) for Black patients and 21.4 (SD 11.1) for White patients (p<0.001). The estimated difference in annual change in mRSS post-MMF treatment compared to pre-treatment was -0.87±0.32 for Black patients, compared to -0.68±0.16 among White patients (p=0.598). Black patients have more severe pulmonary disease at presentation. While Black and White patients have similar rates of change in pFVC and mRSS after MMF exposure, Black patients did not have a meaningful difference in pFVC change post-MMF compared to pre-MMF, suggesting further study is needed in this population.

items.title: Skin-Resident Memory T Cells in Systemic Sclerosis: Immunological Basis, Pathological Mechanisms, and Therapeutic Perspectives.
items.abstract: Skin fibrosis is a hallmark manifestation of systemic sclerosis (SSc) and affects the majority of patients. However, effective therapies capable of reversing or substantially retarding disease progression remain limited due to incomplete understanding of the underlying fibrotic mechanisms. Accumulating evidence indicates that distinct subsets of T lymphocytes play pivotal roles in the inflammation and fibrosis associated with SSc. In particular, tissue-resident memory T (T RM ) cells have emerged as key mediators in chronic inflammatory diseases, with activated CD8 + T RM cells markedly enriched in lesional skin of SSc patients. This review summarizes the immunological basis, key signaling pathways, and potential mechanisms underlying T RM cell involvement in SSc skin fibrosis. Although current evidence remains largely associative and direct causal evidence in humans is still limited, these findings highlight T RM cells as a potentially important therapeutic target. Accordingly, we further discuss emerging strategies targeting T RM cells and related pathways, providing a rationale for precision anti-fibrotic therapy in SSc.

items.title: Development of Potent and Orally Bioavailable MALT1 Inhibitors for Sjögren's Syndrome: Efficacy and Safety Assessment.
items.abstract: MALT1 (mucosa-associated lymphoid tissue lymphoma translocation protein 1) plays a central role in immune cell activation by transducing NF-κB signaling, and its proteolytic activity represents a key node for therapeutic intervention. Previous reports showed that potent MALT1 inhibitor 1 was dominated by very high clearance, which could be linked to amide cleavage. Herein, we report compound 22 , a potent and orally bioavailable inhibitor of MALT1. It was found that introduction of a small methyl substituent could be used to alleviate amide cleavage while maintaining potency, which could be described as a "magic methyl effect." Notably, compound 22 demonstrated excellent pharmacokinetic properties with low clearance and high AUC inf , resulting in in vivo potency (inhibition of germinal center formation) to treat Sjögren's syndrome. However, considering that compound 22 also showed data suggestive of the serious safety risks previously reported by Novartis, we decided to discontinue further research.

items.title: Immune-Mediated Necrotizing Myopathy Across the Age, Autoantibody, Phenotype, Treatment, and Outcome Spectrum: A Systematic Review.
items.abstract: Immune-mediated necrotizing myopathy (IMNM) is a severe idiopathic inflammatory myopathy characterized by prominent myofiber necrosis, weakness, and marked creatine kinase elevation. Anti-3-hydroxy-3-methylglutaryl-coenzyme A reductase (anti-HMGCR) and anti-signal recognition particle (anti-SRP) autoantibodies define clinically relevant subgroups, but uncertainty remains regarding age-related presentation, phenotype, treatment response, and outcomes. The objective of this review was to synthesize published evidence on IMNM using a framework that progresses from IMNM diagnosis to age, autoantibody, phenotype, treatment, and outcomes, emphasizing pediatric and adult disease and antibody-defined heterogeneity. Following the Preferred Reporting Items for Systematic Reviews and Meta-Analyses (PRISMA) 2020 guidelines, a systematic search was conducted across PubMed/MEDLINE, Scopus, ScienceDirect, and Cochrane Central Register of Controlled Trials (CENTRAL) for literature published from 2015 to 2026. Antibody search terms were optional to ensure seronegative disease was not excluded. From 1,541 initially identified records, 66 reports were retained for qualitative synthesis after rigorous screening, full-text eligibility assessment, and risk-of-bias appraisal. Of the 66 retained reports, 78.8% described adult-only and 12.1% pediatric-only populations. The evidence base relies heavily on case-level data, comprising 24 cohorts/comparative studies, 39 case series or reports, and one phase 2 randomized controlled trial (RCT). The single completed RCT (zilucoplan, a complement C5 inhibitor; n = 27, 8 weeks) did not meet its primary efficacy endpoint. Recent literature highlights emerging cardiac, cutaneous, and metabolic manifestations, alongside exploratory use of targeted treatments like chimeric antigen receptor T-cell (CAR-T) and proprotein convertase subtilisin/kexin type 9 (PCSK9) inhibitors. IMNM exhibits substantial clinical heterogeneity by age, autoantibody profile, and phenotype. The dominance of case-level evidence and the negative C5-inhibitor RCT underscore a critical need for adequately powered, mechanistically targeted prospective studies, particularly for pediatric, seronegative, and refractory disease.

items.title: HMGB1 dynamics and expression during neutrophil extracellular trap formation correlate with clinical activity in rheumatoid arthritis.
items.abstract: Rheumatoid arthritis (RA) is a systemic inflammatory condition primarily affecting synovial joints, leading to joint damage and disability. Neutrophils infiltrate the synovium and release neutrophil extracellular traps (NETs). This process involves the release of DNA, histones, and other proteins, including high mobility group box 1 (HMGB1), an "alarmin" amplifying the inflammatory response. The mechanisms that regulate HMGB1 mobilization during NET formation in RA are still unclear. We evaluated the dynamics of HMGB1 during the formation of RA serum-induced NETs and their relationship to markers of disease activity in RA. Patients with RA were classified by American College of Rheumatology/European League Against Rheumatism 2010 criteria. Serum samples were kept at -20 °C. Polymorphonuclear cells were isolated by density gradient centrifugation. Neutrophils were treated with phorbol myristate acetate (PMA), a calcium ionophore (A23187), or serum from patients with RA (SPRA) to induce NET formation. Released DNA was measured by PicoGreen assay and NETs were stained to view HMGB1/DNA under a Leica DM2500 confocal microscope. HMGB1, anti-citrullinated peptides antibodies, and rheumatoid factor were measured by enzyme-linked immunosorbent assay. NETs induction by PMA, A23187, and SPRA caused nuclear morphology changes and DNA release. A23187 and PMA promoted chromatin decondensation with increased nuclear area and extracellular DNA, whereas SPRA induced nuclear decondensation and DNA release. HMGB1 dynamics correlated with nuclear changes and DNA extrusion, with A23187 showing the strongest mobilization. Neutrophils from patients with RA released higher levels of DNA and HMGB1 compared with those from healthy donors, and hmgb1 expression correlated with autoantibodies and disease activity scores. These findings position HMGB1 as a key mediator of NETosis-associated inflammation and a potential biomarker of clinical activity in RA.

items.title: Esomeprazole upregulates Nrf2/HO-1 pathway and attenuates profibrotic response in dermal fibroblasts derived from patients with systemic sclerosis.
items.abstract: To investigate whether esomeprazole attenuates profibrotic responses in dermal fibroblasts from patients with systemic sclerosis (SSc), as well as inflammatory and oxidative stress-related responses in dermal endothelial cells, and to evaluate its effects on nuclear factor erythroid 2-related factor 2 (Nrf2)/heme oxygenase-1 (HO-1) signaling pathway. To evaluate this, primary dermal fibroblasts from patients with limited SSc were stimulated with transforming growth factor-beta 1 (TGF-β1) to induce profibrotic processes and then treated with esomeprazole. Functional studies showed that esomeprazole reversed aberrant fibroblast contractility, and RNA sequencing (RNA-seq) analysis demonstrated that esomeprazole upregulated antioxidant gene networks and downregulated profibrotic pathways. Intriguingly, the upregulation of HO-1 by esomeprazole was blunted upon genetic deletion of the Nrf2 gene. Microvascular injury is an early event in scleroderma and a precursor of fibrosis. As such, we treated microvascular endothelial cells with the prooxidant molecule bleomycin, with and without esomeprazole, and found that esomeprazole attenuated the expression of pro-inflammatory cytokines. Together, these results suggest that esomeprazole upregulates the Nrf2/HO-1 pathway and attenuates profibrotic responses in SSc dermal fibroblasts and reduces inflammatory and oxidative stress-related responses in dermal endothelial cells, supporting further evaluation of the drug in preclinical scleroderma models.

items.title: Neutrophils in spondyloarthritis pathogenesis: from inflammatory infiltration to bone remodeling.
items.abstract: Spondyloarthritis (SpA) is a group of autoimmune diseases characterized by chronic inflammation and pathological new bone formation in the axial skeleton, yet the mechanisms linking inflammatory microenvironment to aberrant osteogenesis remain incompletely understood. Emerging evidence indicates that neutrophils, traditionally viewed as acute inflammatory effectors, play a pivotal role throughout the disease course. Specifically, activated neutrophils can secrete BMPs and may respond to Wnt signaling and they may indirectly promote osteogenic differentiation of mesenchymal stem cells, while NET formation may create a pro-osteogenic niche. The synergistic action of these signals may induce aberrant osteogenic differentiation of mesenchymal stem cells, ultimately contributing to pathological osteophyte formation and spinal ankylosis. This review synthesizes current evidence to propose a testable working model of neutrophil involvement from inflammation initiation to ectopic ossification in SpA, evaluates the therapeutic potential and challenges of targeting neutrophils, and outlines directions for future translational research.

items.title: Case Report: Targeted therapy for TIF1γ-positive dermatomyositis with possible macrophage activation syndrome, cardiac and gastrointestinal involvement: a case-based review.
items.abstract: Dermatomyositis (DM) is an autoimmune disorder characterized primarily by cutaneous and muscular inflammation. Although the TIF1γ antibody-positive variant frequently correlates with an underlying malignancy, instances of severe multisystem compromise lacking a neoplastic association remain exceptionally uncommon. Macrophage activation syndrome (MAS), a lethal cytokine storm, poses substantial diagnostic and therapeutic challenges in DM. Herein, we detail the case of a young man with TIF1γ-positive DM who initially presented with pyrexia, a characteristic exanthema, and myalgia, and then developed rare multisystem complications. Cardiac manifestations, including pericardial effusion and markedly elevated cardiac enzymes, and gastrointestinal complications, including pneumatosis intestinalis and abdominal wall subcutaneous emphysema, were followed by possible MAS, evidenced by sustained high fever and marked increases in inflammatory indices, specifically serum ferritin and interleukin-6 (IL-6). Recognizing the cytokine storm early, the clinical team used alternative diagnostic criteria rather than relying strictly on the HLH-2004 criteria and initiated immediate JAK/IL-6 blockade. Through dynamic surveillance of inflammatory markers, immunosuppressive regimens were meticulously titrated, culminating in successful disease control and a favorable outcome. This case underscores the rarity of simultaneous cardiac and gastrointestinal involvement in TIF1γ-positive DM in the absence of prior immune checkpoint inhibitor exposure. Furthermore, it emphasizes the need for clinical vigilance regarding MAS even when full diagnostic thresholds are not met. The case also highlights the need for vigilant tumor screening and proactive infection surveillance in anti-TIF1γ-positive DM.

items.title: Association of Inflammatory Markers FABP4, S100A12, BMP7, LCN2, and STAT5 With Cardiovascular Disease Risk in Rheumatoid Arthritis Patients: A Cross-Sectional Study.
items.abstract: Persistent systemic inflammation is a hallmark of rheumatoid arthritis (RA) and is closely associated with an increased burden of cardiovascular disease (CVD). Although several inflammatory biomarkers have individually been linked to RA and cardiovascular pathology, their simultaneous associations with conventional cardiovascular risk indicators in the same RA population remain incompletely characterized. This study aimed to investigate the associations between FABP4, S100A12, BMP7, LCN2, and STAT5 and established cardiovascular risk profiles in patients with RA compared with healthy controls. This cross-sectional study included 90 participants: 60 patients with RA (30 treatment-naïve and 30 receiving treatment) and 30 healthy controls. Serum levels of FABP4, S100A12, and BMP7 were measured by ELISA, while mRNA expression of LCN2 and STAT5 was assessed using quantitative real-time PCR. Associations between biomarkers and cardiovascular risk indicators, including Framingham Risk Score (FRS), Systematic Coronary Risk Evaluation (SCORE), high-sensitivity C-reactive protein (HS-CRP), and N-terminal pro-B-type natriuretic peptide (NT-proBNP), were evaluated using correlation and multivariable regression analyses adjusted for age, body mass index, disease activity, and lipid parameters. To reduce the likelihood of false-positive findings, multiple comparisons were adjusted using the false discovery rate (FDR) approach. LCN2 expression was significantly elevated in both treatment-naïve (p = 0.011) and treated RA patients (p = 0.003) compared with controls. FABP4 concentrations were significantly higher in treatment-naïve patients (4.62 ± 0.61 ng/mL) than in treated patients (3.93 ± 0.87 ng/mL) and controls (3.30 ± 1.02 ng/mL). S100A12 levels were also increased in treatment-naïve patients compared with controls, whereas BMP7 and STAT5 did not differ significantly among groups. FABP4 showed weak-to-moderate positive correlations with HS-CRP, NT-proBNP, FRS, and SCORE (r ≈ 0.27-0.49). After FDR correction and multivariable adjustment, only selected associations remained statistically significant, particularly those involving FABP4 with NT-proBNP and HS-CRP and BMP7 with NT-proBNP and DAS-28. In this single-center cross-sectional study, FABP4 and LCN2 showed associations with systemic inflammation and surrogate cardiovascular risk indicators in patients with RA. However, the observed associations were generally modest and should not be interpreted as evidence of causality, CVD progression, or predictive capability. Because cardiovascular risk was evaluated using surrogate risk scores rather than imaging modalities or clinical cardiovascular outcomes, the findings should be considered exploratory. Larger multicenter prospective studies are required to validate these observations and determine whether these biomarkers provide incremental value beyond established cardiovascular risk assessment tools.

items.title: Neuropathic Pain-Like Features in Patients With Rheumatoid Arthritis and Spondyloarthritis Receiving Targeted Therapies: Prevalence and Associated Factors.
items.abstract: Persistent pain despite targeted therapy remains a major challenge in patients with rheumatoid arthritis (RA) and spondyloarthritis (SpA), and neuropathic pain-like features may contribute to this residual pain. We conducted a cross-sectional study including 155 patients receiving biologic or targeted synthetic disease-modifying antirheumatic drugs (bDMARDs or tsDMARDs; 78 RA and 77 SpA) to determine the prevalence of neuropathic pain-like features and identify associated clinical factors. Neuropathic pain-like features were screened using the Douleur Neuropathique 4 (DN4) and painDETECT questionnaires. Univariable logistic regression analyses were performed separately for each disease group, followed by parsimonious multivariable models including functional impairment, disease activity, and current pain intensity. Neuropathic pain-like features (DN4 ≥4) were identified in 19 (24.4%) patients with RA and 21 (27.3%) patients with SpA, with no statistically significant between-group difference (p = 0.679). Although median painDETECT scores were significantly higher in SpA, the distribution of painDETECT categories did not differ significantly between the two groups. In univariable analyses, Health Assessment Questionnaire (HAQ) and current pain visual analogue scale (VAS) were significantly associated with DN4 positivity in RA, whereas Bath Ankylosing Spondylitis Functional Index (BASFI), Ankylosing Spondylitis Disease Activity Score using C-reactive protein (ASDAS-CRP), and current pain VAS were significantly associated with DN4 positivity in SpA. In multivariable analyses, current pain intensity remained significantly associated with DN4 positivity in both disease groups: pain VAS in RA (adjusted OR 2.77, 95% CI 1.54-4.98; p < 0.001) and SpA (adjusted OR 1.90, 95% CI 1.26-2.88; p = 0.002). The adjusted associations with functional impairment and disease activity did not reach statistical significance in either disease group. Neuropathic pain-like features were frequently identified in patients with RA and SpA receiving targeted therapies and were significantly associated with greater pain intensity after adjustment. Associations with functional impairment and inflammatory disease activity remained uncertain after adjustment. These findings support a comprehensive assessment of persistent pain in patients receiving targeted therapies.

items.title: Shared and distinct inflammatory signatures in gout flare and acute CPP crystal arthritis: systemic inflammation persists in gout despite achieving serum urate target.
items.abstract: Gout and calcium pyrophosphate deposition (CPPD) disease cause clinically similar flares and are treated with largely overlapping drugs, yet their systemic inflammatory responses have rarely been compared directly in patients. We compared the circulating inflammatory proteome of both diseases during flares and over time in gout to investigate how these mediators evolve after flare resolution. Proximity extension assay measured 92 inflammation-related proteins in plasma from 71 gout and 86 patients with CPPD during flares, and 96 middle-aged controls. Candidate biomarkers were validated in synovial fluid, crystal-stimulated peripheral blood mononuclear cells (PBMCs) and whole blood, murine air pouch model, and an independent gout cohort. Gout and CPPD flare proteomes were similar, with increased TNFSF14 (false discovery rate [FDR] = 1.49 -24 ), interleukin 6 (FDR = 4.93 -36 ), transforming growth factor-α (FDR = 2.18 -23 ), and colony stimulating factor-1 (FDR = 1.58 -20 ) vs controls. Tumor necrosis factor superfamily member 14 (TNFSF14), previously validated in gout, was detected in CPPD synovial fluid and calcium pyrophosphate (CPP)-stimulated air pouch tissue. In contrast, caspase-8 (CASP-8) was higher in gout than in CPPD during flare (FDR = 7.57 × 10 -12 ). Both monosodium urate and CPP crystals induced CASP-8 in PBMCs and whole blood, whereas CASP-8 inhibition attenuated crystal-induced immune responses. Longitudinally, CASP-8 remained elevated during the intercritical phase and after serum urate target was achieved, showing that its elevation in gout was not flare-restricted. Other persistently altered proteins were enriched in Mitogen-Activated Protein Kinases, tumor necrosis factor, and responses to endogenous stimuli, whereas flare-responsive proteins decreased after flare. Higher CASP-8 was moderately associated with impaired kidney function. TNFSF14 is a candidate shared therapeutic target. CASP-8 distinguished gout from CPPD during flares, whereas its persistence across gout stages supports a broader role in sustained low-grade inflammation.

items.title: Stress Fracture Recovery and Return to Sports in Youth with Juvenile Idiopathic Arthritis.
items.abstract: To compare stress fracture recovery times in children with and without juvenile idiopathic arthritis (JIA), and to evaluate JIA-related factors associated with recovery. This retrospective case-control study included children with JIA <19 years old with a first stress fracture treated at a single center from 2004-2024. Cases were matched 1:3 to children without JIA by age, gender, and fracture location. Recovery time was defined from imaging confirmation of a stress fracture to medical clearance to return to sports. We used a generalized estimating equations method to compare recovery times and evaluate associations with JIA-related factors, including JIA subtype, glucocorticoid and arthritis-directed therapy exposure, and proximity of arthritis to fracture location. The cohort included 260 children (65 cases, 195 controls; 53.8% female; median age 14.3 years [IQR 12.6, 16.2]). Pars interarticularis fractures accounted for 30.8% of injuries, followed by metatarsal (23.1%), and tibial fractures (14.2%). Among children with JIA who sustained pars fractures, 75.0% had an enthesitis-related arthritis (ERA) phenotype. Median recovery times were 10.6 (IQR 7.0, 19.4) weeks for children with JIA and 10.6 (IQR 7.1, 14.6) weeks for controls (P=0.197), with no significant differences for lower-extremity fractures. In contrast, children with JIA who sustained pars fractures had longer recovery times than controls (ratio of geometric means: 1.44, 95% CI 1.01, 2.05; P=0.045). Among children with active sacroiliitis, fractures occurred more frequently in the proximate pars or pelvis than at non-proximate sites (P<0.001). Recovery time was not associated with JIA subtype (all p>0.150), glucocorticoid exposure (P=0.365), or biologic therapy (P=0.625). Overall recovery times did not differ significantly between children with and without JIA. However, children with JIA and pars fractures had longer recovery times, and associations with ERA and sacroiliitis warrant further investigation. Additional research on spondylolysis recovery in young athletes with JIA may help inform individualized return-to-sports recommendations.

items.title: Polygonum aviculare L. and its active compound myricetin inhibit rheumatoid arthritis by targeting the Yes/SHP-2 axis.
items.abstract: Rheumatoid arthritis (RA) is a chronic autoimmune disease characterized by synovial inflammation and joint destruction. Despite therapeutic advances, many patients fail to achieve sustained remission, highlighting the need for more robust treatment options. Fibroblast-like synoviocytes (FLS) are central pathogenic mediators that drive synovial inflammation and joint tissue damage, supporting FLS-targeted therapies as a promising strategy. This study aimed to discover a novel therapeutic plant that suppresses pathogenic FLS responses, identify the major active compound, and elucidate the underlying molecular mechanism, thereby demonstrating their therapeutic potential for RA. 327 plants were screened using synovial cells to identify inhibitors of IL-17-mediated inflammation. Therapeutic efficacy was evaluated in RA patient-derived fibroblast-like synoviocytes (RA-FLS), a 3D synovium-like micromass system, and a collagen-induced arthritis (CIA) mouse model. Transcriptomic analysis was performed to identify key signaling pathways and transcriptional regulators. The active compound was identified through UHPLC-HRMS-based compound profiling and AI-based bioactivity prediction. items.title: Global prevalence and associated factors of thyroid dysfunction in patients with systemic lupus erythematosus: a systematic review and meta-analysis.
items.abstract: Patients with Systemic Lupus Erythematosus (SLE) have a significant association with thyroid dysfunction compared to the general population, yet predisposing factors remain unclear. This systematic review and meta-analysis aims to evaluate the associated factors and prevalence of thyroid dysfunction in patients with SLE. Studies were systematically retrieved from PubMed, Scopus, EBSCO, and Science Direct, up to July 2026. The primary outcome was odds ratios of possible associated factors. Study quality was assessed with Newcastle-Ottawa Scale. Meta-analysis was performed using R. Forty-five studies with 40,627 participants were included. Thyroid dysfunction was a common comorbidity in patients with SLE, with a pooled prevalence of 8.58% for hypothyroidism and 11.11% for subclinical hypothyroidism. Female gender (OR: 2.34; 95% CI: 1.67-3.29), higher SLEDAI score (SMD: 0.69; 95% CI: 0.42-0.96), musculoskeletal (OR: 2.81; 95% CI: 1.39-5.68), and neuropsychiatric (OR: 2.82; 95% CI: 1.63-4.85) involvement, and Anti-thyroglobulin (anti-Tg) (OR: 7.70; 95% CI: 1.03-57.43), were significantly associated though anti-Tg finding should be interpreted with caution due to its wide confidence interval. Meanwhile, IgM/IgG anticardiolipin antibodies (aCL) showed inverse association (OR: 0.43; 95% CI: 0.24-0.76). Thyroid dysfunction, particularly hypothyroidism, is a notable comorbidity in SLE. Demographic factors and commonly used medications do not significantly affect risk. However, female gender, SLEDAI score, and specific clinical manifestations are associated with increased susceptibility. These findings highlight the importance of targeted thyroid monitoring in SLE patients with musculoskeletal or neuropsychiatric involvement.

items.title: Depressive symptoms among adult patients with systemic lupus erythematosus in the Jazan Region, Saudi Arabia: An analytical cross-sectional study.
items.abstract: Mental disorders, including depression, are common among patients with systemic lupus erythematosus (SLE). Depressive symptoms can significantly impair quality of life and are associated with adverse clinical outcomes. Studies investigating depressive symptoms and their associated factors in individuals with SLE have yielded inconsistent findings. Therefore, this study aimed to determine the prevalence of depressive symptoms among patients with SLE and to identify the associated factors in patients from the Jazan Region of Saudi Arabia. An analytical cross-sectional study of 112 patients with SLE in Jazan, Saudi Arabia was conducted in 2023. A convenience sampling technique was used to recruit all eligible adult patients with SLE who attended rheumatology clinics and day-care units at the referral hospitals in the region. Depressive symptoms were assessed using the Patient Health Questionnaire-9 (PHQ-9). Chi-square tests and binary logistic regression analyses were used to examine associations and identify factors associated with depressive symptoms. The majority of participants were female (104 [92.9%]), with ages ranging from 18 to 59 years. Depressive symptoms were present in 80% of participants, with patients experiencing mild depression 25 (22%), moderate depression 28 (25%), moderate-to-severe depression 22 (20%), and severe depression 15 (13%).In the multivariable analysis, although physical activity as a categorical variable did not reach overall statistical significance (global p = 0.067), participants engaging in less than 150 minutes of physical activity per week were significantly less likely to experience depressive symptoms compared with those performing no physical activity (OR = 0.28; 95% CI 0.10-0.82; P = 0.020).In conclusion, depressive symptoms were highly prevalent among patients with SLE in the Jazan Region, and physical activity level was identified as a significant modifiable associated factor in this population. Routine screening could facilitate early detection and intervention in patients with SLE in similar settings, resulting in improved clinical outcomes.

items.title: Myositis as a rare forerunner of Behçet's disease: insights from a new case and review of the literature to unmask a diagnostic trap.
items.abstract: Behcet's disease (BD) is a multisystemic vasculitis classically characterized by a triad of recurrent oral aphtosis, genital ulcers and uveitis. Muscular involvement is rare (described in only about 0.5-3% of cases) and often underrecognized. We report a 59 year old man admitted to our department for myositis, diarrhea, and elevated CPK without mucocutaneous signs. MRI (Magnetic resonance imaging) showed muscle edema, colonscopy reveal intestinal mucosal hyperemia, multiple aphthous ulcers on his sigmoid colon, mild edema and petechiae. BD was diagnosed in one years of follow up when the patient developed oral aphtosis, genital ulcers and HLA-B51 positivity was detected. This case underscores the diagnostic challenge when muscle involvement precedes classical features, complicating the differential diagnosis, and highlights the need to consider BD in unexplained myositis, especially in patients with gastrointestinal symptoms and HLA-B51 positivity. A review of 34 published cases on myositis as an initial manifestation of BD is provided.

items.title: Platelet CLEC-2 as an amplifier of synovial inflammation in rheumatoid arthritis.
items.abstract: Platelets have well-established roles in hemostasis and thrombosis and are increasingly recognized as active regulators of inflammation and immune responses. In rheumatoid arthritis (RA), experimental and clinical studies have implicated platelets in synovial inflammation. Platelet depletion markedly attenuates arthritis in the K/BxN serum-transfer mouse model, and collagen-dependent glycoprotein VI (GPVI) signaling promotes platelet microparticle production, which activates fibroblast-like synoviocytes (FLSs) through interleukin-1 (IL-1). More recently, we reported that platelet C-type lectin-like receptor 2 (CLEC-2) promotes proliferation of fibroblast-like synoviocytes derived from patients with RA (RA-FLSs) in vitro and induces the expression of inflammatory mediators, including IL-6. In the same mouse model, platelet- and megakaryocyte-specific CLEC-2 deficiency suppressed arthritis progression without substantially affecting disease onset. These findings support a role for platelet CLEC-2 in the amplification rather than the initiation of synovial inflammation. This review focuses on the emerging role of platelet CLEC-2 in RA and its relationship with podoplanin-positive FLSs. We discuss platelet access to the synovial compartment, CLEC-2-dependent FLS responses, and the possible relationship between CLEC-2 and other platelet-dependent pathways in synovial inflammation. Taken together, current evidence supports a role for platelet CLEC-2 as an amplifier of ongoing synovial inflammation.

items.title: Identification of IFI44L as a potential immune-associated molecule and theoretical CAR-T target for systemic lupus erythematosus: a cross-platform bioinformatic analysis.
items.abstract: Systemic lupus erythematosus (SLE) is a highly heterogeneous autoimmune disorder characterized by disrupted immune homeostasis, persistent chronic inflammation, and progressive multi-organ injury, accompanied by frequent disease flares and marked interindividual clinical heterogeneity. At present, specific molecular biomarkers for precise evaluation of immune dysregulation and guidance for individualized targeted therapy for SLE remain scarce. This study aimed to screen core genes associated with SLE, explore the correlation between IFI44L and SLE-associated immune disturbance, and validate its diagnostic performance, so as to provide bioinformatic evidence for precise immune diagnosis and targeted intervention of SLE. The GSE72326 microarray dataset was used as the training cohort to screen differentially expressed genes (DEGs) between SLE patients and healthy controls. Gene Ontology (GO), Kyoto Encyclopedia of Genes and Genomes (KEGG) enrichment, and protein-protein interaction (PPI) network analyses were performed to identify core hub genes. The CIBERSORTx algorithm was adopted to quantify peripheral blood immune cell infiltration. Spearman correlation analysis was conducted to assess the association between hub gene expression and immune cell infiltration, and receiver operating characteristic (ROC) curves were plotted to evaluate gene diagnostic efficacy. An independent RNA-seq cohort GSE211700 was used for cross-platform external validation of IFI44L expression patterns and diagnostic efficacy. A total of 104 SLE-related DEGs, including 93 upregulated and 11 downregulated genes, were identified with distinct expression patterns capable of distinguishing SLE patients from healthy controls. Functional enrichment results revealed that DEGs were predominantly enriched in type I interferon response, innate immune activation and inflammatory signaling cascades, consistent with the well-recognized pathological features of SLE. As a key interferon-stimulated gene, IFI44L was selected as the primary target based on integrated transcriptomic profiles and previous mechanistic evidence, despite several other hub genes exhibiting larger expression fold changes. Correlation analysis demonstrated that elevated IFI44L expression was significantly positively correlated with the proportions of M1 macrophages and activated NK cells, and negatively correlated with naive B cells and neutrophils (all P < 0.001). Dual-cohort ROC analysis confirmed the diagnostic potential of IFI44L, with AUCs of 0.9032 in the training cohort and 0.9550 in the independent validation cohort. Consistent with transcriptomic enrichment results, IFI44L may correlate with type I interferon pathway disturbance and abnormal peripheral immune cell infiltration linked to inflammatory manifestations in SLE. Validated across two independent cross-platform cohorts, IFI44L may serve as a non-invasive diagnostic biomarker for SLE. Its potential as a CAR-T target is merely a theoretical conjecture derived from bioinformatic analysis, which provides preliminary clues for subsequent research on individualized treatment of refractory SLE. Key Points • Cross-platform validation using microarray and RNA-seq datasets verified consistent upregulation of peripheral blood IFI44L in SLE patients. • Elevated IFI44L expression correlates with peripheral blood immune cell infiltration disorders and bioinformatically inferred enrichment of type I interferon associated transcriptional signatures in SLE cohorts. • IFI44L exhibits acceptable diagnostic performance for SLE and may serve as a non-invasive blood-based biomarker for SLE. Its potential as a CAR-T target remains only a bioinformatics-derived hypothesis.

items.title: ECMO-assisted valve-in-valve transcatheter aortic valve replacement following surgical aortic valve replacement failure in triple-positive antiphospholipid syndrome and systemic lupus erythematosus-associated libman-sacks endocarditis: a case report.
items.abstract: Libman-Sacks endocarditis (LSE) is a non-infective valvular manifestation of systemic lupus erythematosus (SLE) and antiphospholipid syndrome (APS), affecting 15-30% of patients with APS. Characterized by sterile vegetations predisposing to thromboembolism and valvular dysfunction, optimal anticoagulation and intervention strategies remain challenging, particularly with rapid prosthetic failure. A 63-year-old African American man with a 20-year history of SLE and triple-positive APS presented with cardiogenic shock five months after surgical aortic valve replacement (SAVR) for LSE. Echocardiography revealed severe bioprosthetic obstruction (mean gradient 79.6 mmHg, valve area 0.30 cm²). Given prohibitive redo surgical risk (STS-PROM 18.2%), he underwent ECMO-assisted valve-in-valve transcatheter aortic valve replacement (TAVR) with a 26 mm Edwards SAPIEN 3 valve. Left ventricular ejection fraction improved from 25-29% to 55-59% at 4.5 months, sustained at 50-54% at 8-month follow-up. He remained stable on warfarin (INR 2-3), hydroxychloroquine, and rituximab under multidisciplinary care. This case demonstrates diagnostic challenges differentiating LSE from bioprosthetic valve thrombosis (BPVT); a competing diagnosis that could not be excluded without histopathologic confirmation, critical limitations of DOACs in triple-positive APS, and feasibility of ECMO-supported TAVR as an exceptional rescue strategy. Rituximab was administered for refractory APS, though its independent contribution to the favorable outcome cannot be determined. To our knowledge, this is the first reported ECMO-assisted valve-in-valve TAVR following SAVR failure in APS/SLE-associated LSE. It emphasizes multidisciplinary care, warfarin-based anticoagulation, immunosuppression escalation, and long-term surveillance for complex autoimmune valvular disease.

items.title: Golgi-retained TNFR1 variants induce stress-driven inflammation in a subset of systemic juvenile idiopathic arthritis.
items.abstract: Systemic juvenile idiopathic arthritis (sJIA) is a complex inflammatory disease characterized by recurrent fevers, arthritis, and systemic hyperinflammation; however, its underlying etiology remains poorly understood. Tumor necrosis factor receptor 1 (TNFR1, TNFRSF1A), the prototypical TNF superfamily receptor, signals through its ligand (tumor necrosis factor, TNF) to activate NF-κB-dependent proinflammatory pathways while also promoting cell death. Through family-based and targeted sequencing, we identified multiple rare TNFRSF1A variants, including a de novo truncating variant in a patient with monophasic sJIA. Integrating single cell RNA-seq with in vitro and ex vivo functional assays, we uncovered a patient-specific, unique monocyte population marked by high inflammatory cytokine production. These cells display impaired endosomal and Golgi trafficking, dysregulated autophagy, and increased markers of cellular stress and immune activation. Confocal microscopy revealed aberrant TNFR1 retention within the Golgi apparatus. These monocytes were refractory to LPS-induced cell death, maintained a M1-like inflammatory phenotype and produced proinflammatory cytokines even at steady state. Despite conferring a loss of function in TNFR1 signaling, these variants paradoxically drive a hyperinflammatory phenotype. We propose that this results from combined effects of reduced TNFR1 signaling and cellular stress induced by retention of the mutant receptor in the Golgi.

items.title: ISarcoPRM-Defined Sarcopenia in Radiographic Axial Spondyloarthritis: Beyond Disease-Specific Clinical Factors.
items.abstract: To determine the frequency of ISarcoPRM-defined sarcopenia in men with radiographic axial spondyloarthritis (r-axSpA) versus age-matched male controls and to assess associated disease-specific clinical characteristics. In this single-center, cross-sectional study, 108 men with r-axSpA and 108 age-matched male controls were evaluated. ISarcoPRM-defined sarcopenia required reduced handgrip strength, prolonged Chair Stand Test (CST) time, or both, together with a low sonographic thigh adjustment ratio (sTAR). Conditional logistic regression assessed the association with r-axSpA; multivariable logistic regression examined associated factors within r-axSpA. ISarcoPRM-defined sarcopenia was significantly more frequent in men with r-axSpA than in controls (32.4% vs. 7.4%, P <0.001). The adjusted conditional model showed an association between r-axSpA and ISarcoPRM-defined sarcopenia, although imprecisely estimated (adjusted OR 16.4; 95% CI, 2.5-108.3; P=0.004). Within the r-axSpA group, older age and higher BMI were independently associated with ISarcoPRM-defined sarcopenia, whereas BASMI-lin and ASAS-HI were not independently associated in the adjusted model. ISarcoPRM-defined sarcopenia was more frequent in men with r-axSpA than in age-matched male controls. Interpretation should consider the cross-sectional design, incomplete characterization of cumulative disease burden, and the potential influence of disease-related lower-extremity limitations and BMI adjustment within the ISarcoPRM algorithm.

items.title: Periodontitis Exacerbates Bone Destruction in Rheumatoid Arthritis Through Porphyromonas gingivalis-Induced Carbamylated Neutrophil Extracellular Traps.
items.abstract: Positive correlations between periodontitis and rheumatoid arthritis (RA) are well-documented, yet the underlying causality and mechanisms remain incompletely understood. This study aimed to elucidate the causal role of periodontitis in RA progression and to investigate the mechanisms. Here, we identified carbamylated neutrophil extracellular traps (cNETs), a structure closely associated with bone destruction in RA, as a key mediator. Clinically, synovial samples from RA patients with periodontitis exhibited significantly elevated cNET levels compared to those from periodontally healthy RA patients, and cNET abundance positively correlated with higher rheumatoid factor levels, deeper probing depth and greater clinical attachment loss. In a murine model combining periodontitis and RA, periodontitis exacerbated RA severity, accompanied by increased cNETs formation, particularly upon exposure to Porphyromonas gingivalis. Mechanistically, transcriptomic sequencing and functional assays revealed that cNETs promote osteoclastogenesis and aggravate bone erosion in RA by enhancing RANKL secretion via the MAPK pathway. Therapeutically, chemical inhibition of carbamylation markedly reduced ankle joint inflammation and bone destruction, concomitant with decreased cNET levels and MAPK phosphorylation. Together, our findings establish a causal link between periodontitis and RA aggravation, mediated by P. gingivalis-triggered cNETs that fuel osteoclast formation. Targeting cNETs may thus represent a promising therapeutic strategy for RA.

items.title: Exploring the NETosis-associated immune microenvironment in lupus nephritis: Identification of hub genes, molecular subtypes, and potential diagnostic biomarkers.
items.abstract: Neutrophil extracellular traps (NETs) have been implicated in immune dysregulation in lupus nephritis (LN). However, the expression patterns and potential regulatory roles of NETosis-associated genes in the renal microenvironment remain incompletely characterized. Here, we analyzed transcriptomic data to define a NETosis-associated gene signature and investigate its relationship with immune processes in LN. Publicly available LN transcriptomic datasets were analyzed to identify differentially expressed NETosis-associated genes (DE-NAGs). Functional enrichment analyses were performed, and random forest and least absolute shrinkage and selection operator (LASSO) regression were used to identify hub genes. A LASSO-based diagnostic model was constructed and evaluated using receiver operating characteristic (ROC) curves. Immune-cell infiltration analysis, single-gene gene set enrichment analysis (GSEA), and unsupervised clustering were also performed. Hub-gene expression was further assessed in external datasets and in clinical blood and kidney samples from patients with LN and controls using quantitative PCR (qPCR) and immunohistochemistry (IHC). We identified 23 DE-NAGs enriched in processes related to immune activation, phagocytosis, and reactive oxygen species (ROS) pathways. Nine hub genes showed potential diagnostic value and were associated with immune-cell infiltration and pathways involving immune responses, cytokine signaling, and interferon signaling. Unsupervised clustering based on hub-gene expression identified three molecular subtypes (A, B, and C). External-dataset and experimental validation showed increased expression of DYSF, ITGB2, LILRB2, and TLR2 in blood and kidney samples from patients with LN. The hub genes TLR2, ITGB2/ITGAM, DYSF, and LILRB2, together with the identified molecular subtypes, characterize a NETosis-associated immune microenvironment in LN. These findings provide insight into LN immunopathology and suggest that these genes may have diagnostic and therapeutic relevance, although further validation is required.

items.title: Significant changes in circulating endocannabinoids correlate with disease severity in rheumatoid arthritis: a cross-sectional study.
items.abstract: To investigate alterations in plasma concentrations of circulating endocannabinoids and endocannabinoid-like molecules in patients with rheumatoid arthritis (RA) and to assess their associations with the Disease Activity Score 28 with Erythrocyte Sedimentation Rate (DAS28-ESR). The study was designed as a single-center, cross-sectional investigation. Female patients with RA (n = 43; aged ≥18 years) were recruited at Sheba Medical Center, Israel, and diagnosed according to the 2010 ACR/EULAR classification criteria. Healthy females (n = 38) served as controls. Plasma levels of 25 endocannabinoids and endocannabinoid-like molecules were quantified using solid-phase extraction followed by electrospray ionization liquid chromatography-high-resolution tandem mass spectrometry (ESI-LC-HRMS/MS). Statistical analyses included group comparisons and FDR-corrected linear regression models assessing associations between DAS-28-ESR and metabolite levels, adjusted for age and cannabis use. Several endocannabinoids, including 2-arachidonyl glycerol ether (2-AGE), 2-linoleoyl glycerol (2-LG), 2-oleoyl glycerol (2-OG), 2-palmitoyl glycerol (2-PG), 2-SG, linoleoyl-phenylalanine, linolenic acid (LnA), N-O-leucine, and palmitoylethanolamide (PEA), were significantly elevated in RA patients compared with controls (p = 0.015, p < 0.001, p < 0.001, p < 0.001, p = 0.027, p < 0.001, p = 0.034, p < 0.001, and p = 0.002, respectively). In contrast, anandamide (AEA), N-oleoyl alanine, and O-AEA were significantly reduced (p = 0.012, p < 0.001, and p < 0.001, respectively). Notably, plasma levels of AEA, PEA, and oleoylethanolamide (OEA) correlated significantly with DAS28-ESR scores (p = 0.015, p = 0.008, and p = 0.012, respectively). Specific endocannabinoids and endocannabinoid-like molecules are dysregulated in RA and correlate with disease activity, suggesting potential roles as biomarkers and therapeutic targets.

items.title: [A case of immune-mediated necrotizing myopathy complicated with immune thrombocytopenia successfully treated with intravenous immunoglobulin].
items.abstract: A 41-year-old woman diagnosed with polymyositis had been treated with tacrolimus and repeated an intravenous immunoglobulin (IVIg) over past 14 years, due to worsening symptoms. Preadmission examinations showed thrombocytopenia. We diagnosed with immune thrombocytopenia (ITP) based on positive anti-platelet antibody and increased megakaryocytes on bone marrow examination. Following IVIg, both her muscle weakness and platelet counts normalized. The unique clinical course of this case prompted a reconsideration of her underlying muscular disease. Myopathological reexamination revealed predominantly necrotic and regenerating muscle fibers, and the presence of anti-HMGCR antibodies led to a revised diagnosis of immune-mediated necrotizing myopathy (IMNM) with ITP. Idiopathic inflammatory myopathy combined with ITP has been rarely reported. However, there are no prior reports of IMNM complicated with ITP. If thrombocytopenia is documented during the course of treatment in patients with IMNM, the complication of ITP should be taken into account when formulating the treatment strategy.

items.title: Complement inhibition: a therapeutic turning point in the treatment of recurrent myelitis in a patient with systemic lupus erythematosus.
items.abstract: Systemic lupus erythematosus (SLE) and neuromyelitis optica spectrum disorder (NMOSD) are autoimmune diseases that have been reported to coexist. We describe the case of a 61-year-old woman with long-standing SLE and Sjögren's disease who developed recurrent longitudinally extensive transverse myelitis associated with concomitant NMOSD. Despite treatment with glucocorticoids, plasma exchange, and rituximab, she experienced multiple neurological relapses, with persistent positivity of anti-aquaporin-4 antibodies and magnetic resonance imaging findings consistent with NMOSD, while SLE remained clinically inactive. Therefore, we initiated treatment with an anti-C5 monoclonal antibody for relapse prevention. To our knowledge, this is the first reported case of a patient with coexisting SLE and NMOSD treated with an anti-C5 monoclonal antibody, remaining relapse-free throughout a 22-month follow-up period.

items.title: Salvage Heart Transplantation for Severe Biventricular Failure Associated with Systemic Sclerosis-Rheumatoid Arthritis Overlap Syndrome.
items.abstract: Systemic sclerosis (SSc) is a multisystem autoimmune disease characterized by vasculopathy and fibrosis, and it often affects the heart, leading to ventricular dysfunction, conduction abnormalities, and arrhythmias. Rheumatoid arthritis (RA) is also complicated by pericarditis, valvular heart diseases, and diastolic dysfunction. SSc-associated right ventricular (RV) dysfunction is a rare but life-threatening condition. Herein, we present a case of SSc/RA overlap syndrome associated with catastrophic biventricular failure mimicking arrhythmogenic cardiomyopathy/arrhythmogenic right ventricular cardiomyopathy (ACM/ARVC), requiring central extracorporeal membrane oxygenation (ECMO). Urgent heart transplantation (HTx) successfully saved the patient's life, and he experienced no rejection, allograft dysfunction, or relapse of SSc/RA post-transplant.

items.title: Low-dose CT of the sacroiliac joints in suspected axial spondyloarthritis: Agreement with the rheumatologist's clinical diagnosis at baseline and two-year follow-up.
items.abstract: To assess agreement between baseline low-dose CT (ldCT) findings of the sacroiliac joints (SIJs) and the treating rheumatologist's clinical diagnosis, at baseline and after at least two years of follow-up, in patients clinically suspected of axial spondyloarthritis (axSpA). In this prospective observational study, adults suspected of sacroiliitis underwent ldCT of the SIJs between June 2023 and February 2024 at baseline. Two musculoskeletal radiologists independently evaluated examinations while blinded to clinical data. The rheumatologist's diagnosis at baseline and after at least two years, made with access to ldCT findings, served as comparator; no independent reference standard was available. Agreement with the clinical diagnosis, interobserver agreement and radiation dose were assessed. Seventy-nine patients (53 women, 26 men; mean age 43 years) were included; 25 (32 %) had a clinical axSpA diagnosis at 2 year follow-up. Both comparisons were subject to incorporation bias. Against the baseline clinical diagnosis, ldCT sensitivity was 81 % (95 % CI 57-93) and specificity 83 % (71-90); against the 2-year diagnosis, sensitivity was 80 % (61-91) and specificity 93 % (82-97), with positive and negative predictive values of 83 % and 91 %. Of 11 patients reclassified as axSpA during follow-up, 9 had a positive baseline ldCT. Interobserver agreement was substantial (kappa 0.68). Mean effective dose was 0.45 mSv. ldCT of the SIJs was feasible at radiation doses comparable to conventional radiography and structural lesions were interpreted reproducibly. Agreement with the rheumatologist's diagnosis is likely inflated by incorporation bias. Independent validation is required before changing imaging pathways.

items.title: Anti-NOR-90 autoantibodies and clinical associations in systemic sclerosis: an international retrospective cohort study.
items.abstract: Autoantibodies against NOR-90 are rare and have been associated with systemic sclerosis (SSc). This study seeks to identify the characteristics of SSc participants with anti-NOR-90 autoantibodies. An international (Canada, Australia, USA, Mexico) cohort of 2143 SSc participants was included. Sera were tested using a line immunoassay (Euroimmun, Lübeck, Germany). Clinical associations with anti-NOR-90 autoantibodies were investigated. Single-specificity anti-NOR-90-positive was defined as anti-NOR-90-positivity without other SSc-related autoantibodies, except for anti-Ro52/TRIM21. 115 (5%) participants were anti-NOR-90-positive, of whom the majority overlapped with other autoantibodies. Anti-NOR-90 positivity overall was associated with a higher frequency of calcinosis (35% vs. 24%, OR 1.70, 95% CI: 1.13, 2.52), digital ulcers (62% vs. 49%, OR 1.70, 95% CI: 1.12, 2.61) and arthritis (37% vs. 29%, OR 1.61, 95% CI: 1.06, 2.40). Single-specificity anti-NOR-90-positive participants (n = 21) a significantly lower mean % predicted forced vital capacity (FVC, 82.0% vs. 91.3%) and diffusing capacity (DLCO, 58.9% vs. 69.0%), and a trend toward higher prevalence of interstitial lung disease (61% vs. 40%, OR 2.36, 95% CI: 0.92, 6.45) and lower median mRSS (4.0 vs. 7.0). Anti-NOR-90 autoantibodies were not associated with increased cancer (10% vs. 8%) or mortality (adjusted HR 1.28, 95% CI: 0.92, 1.79, log rank p = 0.3). Results from sensitivity analyses excluding anti-Ro52/TRIM21 from single-specificity definition were consistent in direction and magnitude. In this large multicentre cohort, anti-NOR-90 autoantibodies commonly overlapped with other SSc-autoantibodies. Single-specificity anti-NOR-90 positivity was associated with more frequent interstitial lung disease and a tendency for lower mRSS.

items.title: Precision nutrition for rheumatoid arthritis management: integrating nutrigenomics, epigenetics, multi-omics, and artificial intelligence.
items.abstract: Plant-based diets have been garnering increasing attention for their ability to reshape gut microbiota, reduce systemic inflammation, and alleviate joint pain in rheumatoid arthritis (RA). However, dietary responses are not uniform, as substantial inter-individual variability arises from genetic polymorphisms, metabolic diversity, and immune heterogeneity. In some patients, specific foods may exacerbate disease activity, emphasizing the need to identify personal dietary triggers and implement individualized nutritional strategies. Nutrigenomics, which integrates nutrition with genetic profiling, provides a valuable framework for understanding the influence of genetic variants on nutrient absorption, metabolism, inflammatory signaling, and immune regulation. Notably, dietary bioactive compounds can also modulate RA pathogenesis through epigenetic mechanisms, including DNA methylation, histone modifications, and microRNA-mediated regulation, thereby altering gene expression programs associated with autoimmunity and chronic inflammation. Diet-derived metabolites and microbial products further interact with host genomic and epigenomic networks, creating a dynamic nutrient-gene-microbiome axis that shapes RA susceptibility, disease severity, and therapeutic responsiveness. Recent advances in multi-omics technologies, including genomics, epigenomics, transcriptomics, proteomics, metabolomics, and microbiome profiling, have offered deeper insights into nutrient-driven molecular pathways and immune dysregulation in RA. These findings enable precision dietary interventions enriched with anti-inflammatory nutrients and functional bioactive to improve symptom control and long-term outcomes. Artificial intelligence (AI) offers an emerging strategy by integrating multi-omics, clinical, and dietary data to generate actionable personalized nutrition approaches. This review highlights current evidence on nutrigenomic and epigenetic regulation in RA and discusses AI-driven precision nutrition as a future strategy to enhance disease management and patient wellbeing.
