items.title: Interleukin-12 Is Associated with Rheumatoid Factor and Interferon-γ, but Not with Disease Activity, in Patients with Rheumatoid Arthritis.
items.abstract: Background: IL-12 is a proinflammatory cytokine produced mainly by activated dendritic cells and macrophages that drives the differentiation of naïve T cells into Th1 cells and stimulates interferon-γ production by natural killer and T cells, thereby linking innate and adaptive immunity. Ultrasensitive quantification of IL-12 has not previously been performed in large rheumatoid arthritis (RA) cohorts, mainly due to the limited availability and high cost of these platforms. In the present study, we measured serum IL-12 using an ultrasensitive assay to systematically assess its relationship with key disease characteristics in a large, well-characterized cohort of patients with RA. Methods: A total of 216 patients with RA were recruited and underwent a comprehensive assessment of disease characteristics and disease activity. Lipid parameters and hematological markers were assessed, insulin resistance indices were calculated, and metabolic syndrome was defined according to established criteria. Arterial stiffness, carotid intima-media thickness, and plaque presence were evaluated through carotid ultrasonography. Serum IL-12 levels were quantified using Simoa (Single Molecule Array) technology. To examine the relationship between clinical and metabolic parameters and IL-12 concentrations, multivariable linear regression models were applied. Results: In multivariable analyses, serum IL-12 levels were independently associated with IFN-γ and rheumatoid factor positivity. However, no significant relationships were found between IL-12 and disease activity indices, acute-phase reactants, cardiovascular risk factors, subclinical atherosclerosis, lipid profile, glucose metabolism, or hematological parameters. Conclusions: Using an ultrasensitive assay, we found that serum IL-12 levels were associated with interferon-γ levels and rheumatoid factor positivity in patients with RA, supporting a role for IL-12 at the interface between cellular and humoral immunity. In contrast, circulating IL-12 did not appear to be a useful systemic biomarker of disease activity or of the cardiovascular and hematological comorbidities associated with RA.

items.title: ADAM-10 Is Involved in Osteoblast Mineralization and Rheumatoid Arthritis-Associated Bone Destruction.
items.abstract: Rheumatoid arthritis (RA), a chronic autoimmune condition, causes irreversible bone destruction. A disintegrin and metalloprotease 10 (ADAM-10) has been implicated in inflammatory processes in RA. We investigated the potential role of ADAM-10 in osteoblast mineralization and RA-associated bone destruction. Serum ADAM-10 levels in RA patients were measured by ELISA, and ADAM-10 expression in osteoblasts was assessed by Western blotting. Collagen-induced arthritis (CIA) mice were treated intraperitoneally with the ADAM-10 inhibitor GI254023X (100 mg/kg) for three weeks. Arthritis and bone destruction were evaluated by macroscopic, immunohistochemical, histological, and micro-CT analyses. The effects of ADAM-10 inhibition on primary osteoblast mineralization were also assessed by Alizarin Red S staining. Serum ADAM-10 levels in patients with RA tended to be higher at Stage III of the Steinbrocker classification. In CIA mice, ADAM-10 inhibition attenuated weight loss, paw swelling, and arthritis scores and suppressed bone destruction. ADAM-10 inhibition also significantly reduced Rankl expression in knee joints. Furthermore, the inhibition reversed the suppression of primary osteoblast mineralization induced by TNF-α. Pharmacological inhibition of ADAM-10 attenuated experimental arthritis and bone destruction and improved osteoblast mineralization, suggesting that ADAM-10 may contribute to inflammatory bone destruction in RA.

items.title: Natural Products for Rheumatoid Arthritis Therapy: Research Progress and Translational Perspectives.
items.abstract: Rheumatoid arthritis (RA) is a chronic autoimmune disease characterized by persistent synovial inflammation, progressive joint destruction, and substantial systemic complications. Although current pharmacological therapies have improved disease control, important unmet needs for RA remission remain owing to the incomplete response, loss of efficacy, long-term safety concerns, limited capacity for tissue repair, and barriers related to accessibility and adherence. Against this background, natural products have emerged as an important area of interest in RA therapy research because many of them can modulate multiple components of the pathogenic network, including immune dysregulation, synovial inflammation, oxidative stress, and structural damage. Therefore, this review provides an updated overview of natural products for RA treatment, with emphasis on their therapeutic effects, mechanistic basis, and translational potential as well as key challenges. In particular, we discuss the natural-product research in RA therapy along an evolving continuum, from traditionally used complex natural products, such as herbal medicines and venom-based preparations, to structurally defined bioactive compounds, including flavonoids, alkaloids, terpenoids, and polysaccharides. The review further summarizes the principal pharmacological actions of these agents, their advantages and limitations in anti-RA intervention, and current strategies to enhance their development, including formulation optimization, delivery systems, and mechanism-guided translational approaches.

items.title: Diagnostic and Clinical Utility of Novel Anti-PAD4 Antibodies in Anti-CCP2-Negative and Anti-CCP2-Positive Rheumatoid Arthritis.
items.abstract: Background/Objectives: Diagnosis of rheumatoid arthritis (RA) remains challenging, particularly in anti-CCP2-negative disease. Novel biomarkers, including anti-peptidyl arginine deiminase 4 (PAD4) autoantibodies, have emerged as promising tools for improving diagnostic accuracy in RA patients. The aim of this study was to analyze the performance of the first clinically validated anti-PAD4 assay. Methods: A total of 192 well-characterized RA patients and 383 controls were included in this study and tested for anti-CCP2, RF IgA, and RF IgM (all Phadia, Thermo Fisher) as well as anti-PAD4 IgA and anti-PAD4 IgG by ELISA (laboratory developed test, Exagen, Inc., Vista, CA, USA). Results for the anti-PAD4 IgG ELISA for 143 patients were used for method comparison with a particle-based multi-analyte technology (PMAT, Inova Diagnostics, San Diego, CA, USA). Results : ELISA and PMAT showed moderate-to-good agreement for anti-PAD4 IgG (rho = 0.66; Passing-Bablok slope 0.83, 95% CI 0.71-0.92; kappa = 0.67). Anti-PAD4 IgG was significantly correlated with anti-PAD4 IgA (rho = 0.47) and weakly correlated with RF IgM (rho = 0.29), RF IgA (rho = 0.28), and anti-CCP2 (rho = 0.22) (all p < 0.001). The PAD4 IgG and IgA ELISAs were validated in the RA population, yielding sensitivities/specificities of 31.8%/92.7% for anti-PAD4 IgG, 18.8%/93.7% for anti-PAD4 IgA, 43.2%/91.1% for RF IgM, 23.4%/96.1% for RF IgA, and 42.2%/99.2% for anti-CCP2, respectively. Anti-CCP2 IgG achieved the highest discriminatory performance (AUC = 0.86), followed by RF IgA (AUC = 0.69) and RF IgM (AUC = 0.67). Anti-PAD4 IgG and anti-PAD4 IgA showed modest discrimination (AUC = 0.55 and 0.52, respectively). items.title: Developing an Algorithm to Quantify Dermatomyositis-Associated Calcinosis Using Infrared Images.
items.abstract: Background/Objectives : Adult and Juvenile Dermatomyositis (DM/JDM)-associated calcinosis varies in its clinical presentations. Current modalities such as physician exam and CT imaging do not fully document calcinosis burden. As a result, this paper examines infrared imaging, which measures skin temperature, as a supplementary modality to assess calcinosis activity. Methods : Fifteen patients (3 DM and 12 JDM) who fulfilled probable or definite Bohan and Peter criteria for DM/JDM and with previously documented calcinosis were included. IR scans of target body regions were obtained in a temperature-controlled and humidity-monitored room. We developed an algorithm to assess calcinosis by measuring local temperature variations in IR scans. Body regions were determined to be calcinosis-positive if the algorithm identified at least 15% of the body region as suspected calcinosis. Results : Twenty-nine out of ninety body regions were designated calcinosis-positive. The average suspected calcinosis areas ranged from 8.6 to 14.2%, and left and right extremity averages were within 0.6% area of each other. Agreement between the IR algorithm and physician exam was variable, as the algorithm simultaneously detected regions that overlapped with physician-marked areas and regions outside of physician-marked boundaries. Conclusions : IR imaging appears to identify areas of calcinosis activity in DM/JDM and presents many promising advantages to warrant future study. Its integration with structural imaging modalities will enable a more comprehensive assessment of calcinosis.

items.title: NLRP3 inflammasome and Sjögren disease: mechanisms, clinical associations and therapeutic prospects.
items.abstract: Sjögren disease (SjD; formerly referred to as Sjögren syndrome) is a chronic autoimmune disease characterized by exocrine gland dysfunction and systemic immune abnormalities. In recent years, clinical and preclinical studies have suggested that dysregulation of the NOD-like receptor family pyrin domain-containing 3 (NLRP3) inflammasome may contribute to inflammatory responses, glandular damage, and disease progression in SjD, although the available human evidence remains primarily associative. This review summarizes alterations in the NLRP3 inflammasome in patients with SjD, animal models, and cell models; discusses its upstream regulation, downstream effects, associated clinical phenotypes, and systemic involvement; and compares evidence across different cell types, disease stages, and therapeutic interventions. Based on current evidence, NLRP3 is more likely to function as an inflammatory amplification and regulatory node in the context of pre-existing autoimmunity and tissue stress, with its role varying according to cell type, disease status, and the local microenvironment. NLRP3 and its related pathways therefore have potential therapeutic value; however, evidence for direct targeting of NLRP3 in SjD remains largely limited to preclinical studies, whereas some immunomodulatory drugs supported by clinical studies are not NLRP3-specific therapies. Further clarification of the cell-specific and stage-specific roles of NLRP3, together with identification of patient subgroups that may benefit, will be critical for promoting its clinical translation.

items.title: From metabolic reprogramming to immune homeostasis: the bidirectional regulatory network of HIF-1 α /HK2 and Th17/Treg in gout.
items.abstract: Gout is a metabolic inflammatory disease whose pathogenesis involves the complex interaction between metabolic reprogramming and immune homeostasis imbalance. This review focuses on the bidirectional network through which the HIF-1 α /HK2 axis regulates the Th17/Treg balance via glycolytic reprogramming. Monosodium urate (MSU) crystals drive enhanced aerobic glycolysis in macrophages through the GLUT1-JNK-HIF-1 α signaling axis, where hexokinase 2 (HK2), as a metabolic checkpoint, connects glycolysis with NLRP3 inflammasome activation and neutrophil extracellular trap (NETosis)-induced M1 polarization. The glycolytic metabolic bias promotes the differentiation of T helper 17 (Th17) cells while inhibiting the generation of regulatory T (Treg) cells. In turn, cytokines derived from Th17/Treg cells reversely regulate the metabolic status of antigen-presenting cells, forming a feedback loop for inflammation amplification or resolution. Based on this network model, intervention strategies targeting the HIF-1 α /HK2/mTOR glycolytic axis and metabolic checkpoints (such as HK2, PKM2), including chaetocin, rapamycin, and various natural products, have shown therapeutic potential for restoring immune homeostasis. Current evidence mainly comes from animal models and in vitro experiments. In the future, it is necessary to use single-cell multi-omics technology to resolve the heterogeneity of the immunometabolic landscape, and to verify the dynamic regulatory mechanism of this network in the self-limiting resolution of gout inflammation.

items.title: Tissue factor-associated neutrophil extracellular traps in dermatomyositis: procoagulant activity and endothelial activation in vitro .
items.abstract: Dermatomyositis (DM) is an immune-mediated myopathy characterized by inflammatory and vascular manifestations and variable systemic involvement; however, the interplay among neutrophil activation, complement, and coagulation remains unclear. We investigated whether serum from patients with DM induces tissue factor (TF)-associated neutrophil extracellular traps (NETs) and examined their functional effects in vitro . Serum from seven patients with active DM and seven matched healthy individuals was analyzed for inflammatory mediators, citrullinated histone H3 (CitH3), thrombin-antithrombin (TAT) complexes, soluble C5b-9, and DNase-I activity. Control neutrophils were exposed to DM serum and, then, NET formation, TF expression and activity, and thrombin generation were assessed. Inhibition experiments targeting complement, TF, and NETs were performed. Co-culture experiments assessed endothelial activation, while skin biopsies were examined by immunofluorescence. Patients with DM exhibited increased inflammatory mediators, CitH3, TAT complexes, and soluble C5b-9, together with reduced DNase-I activity. DM serum induced TF expression and release of TF-associated NETs by control neutrophils. DNase-I and eculizumab reduced NET formation, while eculizumab additionally decreased TF mRNA expression and NET-associated TF activity. TF-associated NETs promoted adhesion molecule expression by human aortic endothelial cells, an effect attenuated by DNase-I or TF neutralization. TF-positive NET fragments were detected in lesional DM skin but not healthy skin. These exploratory findings support a contribution of C5-dependent complement activation to TF-associated NET formation and show that these NETs can enhance thrombin generation and endothelial activation in vitro . Their relationship to clinical vasculopathy or thrombotic risk remains unknown, providing evidence for potential links between inflammation, thrombosis, and vascular injury in DM.

items.title: A fatal threat: Pneumocystis jirovecii pneumonia with rapidly progressive interstitial lung disease in anti-MDA5-positive dermatomyositis-a case report.
items.abstract: Pneumocystis jirovecii pneumonia (PJP) is a respiratory infection caused by Pneumocystis organisms, representing an opportunistic fungal infection. The clinical occurrence of PJP combined with rapidly progressive interstitial lung disease (RP-ILD) in dermatomyositis (DM) have also been reported occasionally, but patients with this combination of conditions experience rapid disease progression and high mortality rates. We reported a 70-year-old female patient with dyspnea and fever, detailing her laboratory tests, computed tomography (CT) findings and bronchoalveolar lavage fluid findings. The patient's main clinical manifestations were dyspnea and fever. CT scans revealed scattered reticular opacities and ground-glass opacities in both lungs and metagenomic next-generation sequencing (mNGS) of the bronchoalveolar lavage fluid detected Pneumocystis jirovecii. Laboratory tests revealed positive anti-MDA5 antibodies during hospitalization. The patient was treated with high-flow oxygen therapy and methylprednisolone upon admission. Subsequently, the patient received mechanical ventilator support and was administered trimethoprim-sulfamethoxazole (TMP-SMX), plasma exchanges and immunoglobulin treatment. The patient's fever subsided, but respiratory failure and interstitial lung disease continued to progressively worsen. Ground-glass opacities, mixed ground-glass opacities, consolidations and reticular opacities were significantly more pronounced than on admission, indicating RP-ILD changes post-treatment. The patient succumbed after 13 days of treatment. PJP complicated by rapidly progressive interstitial lung disease can be fatal in patients, emphasizing the critical importance of early identification of PJP and prompt initiation of anti-PJP treatment. It is crucial to recognize that some MDA5+ DM patients may not present with the typical rash, and in certain cases, RP-ILD may be the primary manifestation. Therefore, early screening for anti-MDA5 antibodies is essential for patients presenting with unexplained early-stage RP-ILD.

items.title: Isotype-dependent shifts of natural autoantibody profiles in systemic lupus erythematosus-associated serological groups.
items.abstract: Homeostatic natural autoantibodies (nAAbs) are proposed regulators of inflammation and autoimmunity, studied mainly as natural IgM. Whether pathological autoantibody (pAAb) expansion in systemic lupus erythematosus (SLE)-associated serology is mirrored by isotype-divergent nAAb changes has rarely been examined. pAAb positivity and co-positivity ratios (exact 95% confidence intervals) and intersection (UpSet) analyses were derived from a regional diagnostic cohort (Southern Transdanubia, Hungary, 2014-2024; 128,847 enzyme-linked immunosorbent assay (ELISA) results, 73,747 pseudonymised patients). The dominant patterns defined anti-double-stranded DNA (a-dsDNA)/anti-nucleosome-, anti-SSA/Ro- and anti-cardiolipin/β2-glycoprotein I (a-CL/β2GPI)-dominant and co-positive groups, each verified against serological follow-up. In 110 residual sera, IgG and IgM nAAbs against citrate synthase (CS) and heat shock proteins (HSP) 60 and 70 were measured by ELISA and compared by Kruskal-Wallis and Dunn-Holm tests. Of a-dsDNA IgG-positive patients, 30.36% carried an additional disease-specific pAAb, along two largely separate axes, antiphospholipid (15.90%) and extractable nuclear antigen-associated (16.51%); anti-neutrophil cytoplasmic antibody co-positivity was rare (3.02%), and 42.01% showed a-nucleosome co-reactivity. a-CS IgM was reduced in every pAAb-positive group (all p Holm < 0.001), whereas increased a-CS, a-HSP60 and a-HSP70 IgG levels were confined to a-dsDNA/a-nucleosome-containing (chromatin-reactive) profiles (a-CS IgG, p Holm ≤ 0.012). These shifts were robust to sex-, age- and measurement-year adjustment. Isotype-resolved nAAb profiling anchored in diagnostic serology revealed a counter-directional shift (IgM↓ across pAAb-positive groups, IgG↑ in chromatin-reactive profiles). These hypothesis-generating findings are consistent with impaired homeostatic IgM-mediated regulation and with class-switched IgG nAAb reactivity as a marker of B-cell activation, and warrant clinical and functional validation in prospective cohorts.

items.title: Association of the Pan-Immune-Inflammation Value with Persistent Proteinuria in Patients with Familial Mediterranean Fever.
items.abstract: Background and Objectives: Persistent proteinuria is an important marker of renal involvement in familial Mediterranean fever (FMF). This study investigated the association between the pan-immune-inflammation value (PIV) and persistent proteinuria, evaluated the discriminatory performance of PIV, the neutrophil-to-lymphocyte ratio (NLR), and monocyte-to-HDL cholesterol ratio (MHR), and identified factors independently associated with persistent proteinuria. Materials and Methods: This retrospective cross-sectional study included 190 adults with FMF and 150 healthy controls. Persistent proteinuria was defined as a spot urine protein-to-creatinine ratio (UPCR) > 20 mg/mmol confirmed on at least two measurements obtained at least 1 week apart. PIV quartile analysis, Spearman correlation, ROC analysis, and multivariable logistic regression were performed. Results: Persistent proteinuria was present in 62 (32.6%) patients with FMF. Its prevalence increased progressively across PIV quartiles ( p for trend < 0.001), and PIV was positively correlated with UPCR (ρ = 0.298, p < 0.001). PIV showed an AUC of 0.774, compared with 0.658 for NLR and 0.654 for MHR. In multivariable analysis, PIV (OR 1.006, 95% CI 1.002-1.009, p = 0.001) and homozygous M694V genotype (OR 3.39, 95% CI 1.46-7.86, p = 0.004) were independently associated with persistent proteinuria. Conclusions: PIV and homozygous M694V genotype were independently associated with persistent proteinuria. PIV may serve as an adjunctive biomarker for the assessment of persistent proteinuria in patients with FMF, although prospective multicenter studies are needed to determine its clinical utility.

items.title: Machine Learning Models to Predict Methotrexate Treatment Response in Rheumatoid Arthritis: A Scoping Review.
items.abstract: Methotrexate (MTX) remains the anchor drug in rheumatoid arthritis (RA) despite the advent of newer disease-modifying anti-rheumatic drugs (DMARDs) that have transformed the treatment landscape of RA. A significant proportion of patients fail to respond to MTX monotherapy. Machine learning (ML) methods have identified predictors of the MTX response to refine RA treatment strategies. Objective: This scoping review (ScR) aimed to provide a comprehensive overview of the current landscape of ML applications for predicting the MTX response in RA. Methods: A thorough online search in PubMed and Web of Science databases identified studies using ML to predict MTX treatment responses in RA. We extracted and synthesised data on study design, ML methodologies, data sources, and outcomes. Findings were summarised descriptively. Of the 266 articles identified, 14 studies met the inclusion criteria. Data sources included electronic medical records, clinical and genetic biomarkers. Results: ML models primarily employed supervised techniques (e.g., random forests, logistic regression). Most clinical studies consistently identified baseline DAS28 as the strongest predictor of response to MTX. Other clinical predictors included Health Assessment Questionnaire (HAQ) scores, erythrocyte folate, lymphocyte count, platelet count, anti-citrullinated protein antibodies (ACPA), and rheumatoid factor (RF). Several genotypes (e.g., ABCB1 rs1045642 and ABCC3 rs4793665) and single nucleotide polymorphisms (SNPs), i.e., (pfcHap), were reported as predictors. Conclusions: Higher baseline disease activity based on DAS28 was the most common predictor of poor response across the clinical studies.

items.title: Association of the CALLY Index with Short-Term Treatment Response in Ankylosing Spondylitis.
items.abstract: Background/Objectives: We examined the association between the pretreatment C-reactive protein-albumin-lymphocyte (CALLY) index and three-month clinical response to advanced therapy in patients with ankylosing spondylitis. Methods: We retrospectively analyzed 209 patients with ankylosing spondylitis who received biologic or targeted synthetic disease-modifying antirheumatic drugs. Laboratory measurements and Bath Ankylosing Spondylitis Disease Activity Index (BASDAI) scores were recorded at baseline; BASDAI was reassessed at three months. Response was defined as a reduction of at least 50% in BASDAI (BASDAI50). Analyses included Spearman's rank correlation, multivariable logistic regression, nonlinear spline modeling, and receiver operating characteristic (ROC) analysis. Results: Among 209 patients, 167 (79.9%) achieved BASDAI50 response. Following recalculation from the recorded laboratory measurements, baseline CALLY was associated with treatment response, with a nonlinear exposure-response relationship (spline versus linear likelihood-ratio χ 2 = 26.27, df = 2; p < 0.001; overall association p < 0.001). The CALLY AUC was 0.763 (95% bootstrap CI: 0.671-0.852), compared with 0.773 for CRP (paired bootstrap p = 0.485). The apparent and optimism-corrected AUCs of the adjusted spline model were 0.786 and 0.753, respectively. Conclusions: Baseline CALLY was nonlinearly associated with three-month BASDAI50 response and showed moderate discrimination between responders and nonresponders in this cohort. It did not demonstrate incremental value beyond CRP. Its clinical predictive utility remains unestablished and requires external validation.

items.title: α-Ketoglutarate Alleviates the Pathogenesis of Systemic Lupus Erythematosus via Reducing Oxidative Stress and Attenuating Excessive Immune Response.
items.abstract: Systemic lupus erythematosus (SLE) is a systemic autoimmune disease driven by dysregulated immune activation, with heterogeneous clinical manifestations and multi-organ injury. α-ketoglutarate (AKG) is a key intermediate metabolite of the tricarboxylic-acid cycle (TCA), participating in various physiological processes, including energy metabolism and immune regulation. In this study, 8-week-old female BALB/c mice were injected with pristane to establish an SLE mouse model. Using this model, we explored the therapeutic function and underlying mechanism of AKG intervention on SLE. AKG administration significantly reduced serum antinuclear antibody (ANA) levels and alleviated renal injuries and biochemical improvement in SLE mice. Furthermore, it effectively maintained glomerular integrity and decreased the serum levels of biochemical enzymes and indices. Meanwhile, oxidative stress was ameliorated associated with the capacity of endogenous antioxidant enzymes and reducing the level of malondialdehyde (MDA). Most importantly, AKG upregulated the transcriptional levels of genes related to mitochondrial respiratory-chain complex, and increasing the production of adenosine triphosphate (ATP) in kidney tissues. Moreover, AKG administration regulated the proportion of spleen immune cells, and improved inflammation by decreasing the Interferon-stimulated genes (ISGs) expression levels, suppressing the liberation of inflammatory cytokines, ultimately alleviating SLE-associated damage. In summary, AKG protects against SLE through multi-targeted pathways, including suppressing oxidative stress, improving mitochondrial biogenesis-related factors, modulating immune-cell profiles, and dampening inflammatory response. These findings indicate that AKG has the effect of improving SLE.

items.title: Adipocytokine Profiling and Cardiovascular Risk Stratification in Rheumatoid Arthritis: Literature Review.
items.abstract: Rheumatoid arthritis (RA) is associated with an increased burden of cardiovascular disease (CVD), reflecting interactions among persistent systemic inflammation, traditional cardiometabolic risk factors, and treatment exposure. Conventional risk scores may underestimate cardiovascular risk in some patients with RA. This narrative review examines the potential role of adipokines in linking synovial inflammation and metabolic dysfunction to vascular disease. It discusses the context-dependent cardiovascular associations of adiponectin, the pro-inflammatory signaling of leptin, resistin, visfatin, and chemerin, and the proposed protective roles of omentin, vaspin, and apelin. Emerging observations connect adipokine profiles with measures of subclinical atherosclerosis and selected clinical outcomes; however, methodological heterogeneity and residual confounding constrain causal and prognostic interpretations. We also consider venous thromboembolism, cardiometabolic multimorbidity, and treatment-related risk, including the clinical safety context of JAK inhibitors. At present, adipokine profiling remains investigational and should complement research, not replace established cardiovascular risk assessment and control of disease activity and conventional risk factors.

items.title: Do Non-Invasive Fibrosis Indices Reflect Interstitial Lung Disease and Pulmonary Function in Systemic Sclerosis?
items.abstract: Background/Objectives : Interstitial lung disease (ILD) is a major manifestation of systemic sclerosis (SSc). The Fibrosis-4 index (FIB-4) and aspartate aminotransferase-to-platelet ratio index (APRI) are indirect hepatic fibrosis indices of uncertain pulmonary relevance. We compared these indices by documented ILD status and explored associations with pulmonary function and historical forced vital capacity (FVC) changes. Methods : This retrospective observational study included 102 patients with SSc (61 with ILD, 41 without ILD). Indices were calculated from the last eligible laboratory assessment; ILD was classified using available high-resolution computed tomography records. Patients with relevant hepatic and laboratory confounders were excluded. Pulmonary associations were explored within SSc-ILD, including a sensitivity analysis restricted to ≤12 months between laboratory and follow-up pulmonary function testing. Results : Neither index differed significantly by ILD status (FIB-4, p = 0.91; APRI, p = 0.06). In logistic models adjusted for age and diffuse cutaneous phenotype, FIB-4 showed a borderline inverse association with documented ILD status only after adjustment for age and and diffuse cutaneous phenotype (adjusted odds ratio 0.247, 95% confidence interval 0.062-0.988; p = 0.048), whereas APRI did not ( p = 0.064). Within SSc-ILD, neither index correlated significantly with FVC % predicted, diffusing capacity for carbon monoxide (DLCO) % predicted, forced expiratory volume in 1 s (FEV1) % predicted, or historical FVC changes. FIB-4 correlated inversely with absolute FVC (ρ = -0.53, p < 0.001), but this association was not significant after age and sex adjustment ( p = 0.40). The absolute-FVC correlation persisted within the ≤12-month subgroup. Conclusions : Findings do not consistently support these indices as stand-alone indicators of SSc pulmonary involvement; prospective validation is needed.

items.title: IgA-Expressing Cells at the Human Ocular Surface and Reduced Tear IgA2 Abundance in Schirmer Strip Extracts from Patients with Dry Eye Disease and Primary Sjögren's Syndrome.
items.abstract: This study investigated the distribution of IgA-expressing cells in human ocular tissues and IgA subclass profiles in Schirmer strip extracts from patients with dry eye disease (DED) and primary Sjögren's syndrome (pSS). Immunofluorescence staining was performed on paraffin-embedded lacrimal gland, conjunctival, and corneal tissues from body donors. Independently, Schirmer strip extracts from healthy controls ( n = 18), patients with DED ( n = 75), and patients with pSS ( n = 10) were analyzed. Total protein concentrations were determined using a bicinchoninic acid assay, while total IgA, IgA1, and IgA2 were quantified by ELISA and normalized to total protein. CD38 + and CD38 - IgA-expressing cells were detected in the lacrimal gland and conjunctival stroma, with IgA1-expressing cells predominating over IgA2-expressing cells. No IgA-positive cells were detected in the examined corneal sections. Total protein concentrations were lower in pSS than in DED. Normalized IgA2 abundance was reduced in both DED and pSS compared with controls, while normalized total IgA was additionally reduced in pSS. Unnormalized extract concentrations showed broadly similar patterns. These independent findings demonstrate differences in recovered IgA subclass profiles, although differences in collection materials and patient characteristics preclude attributing these alterations exclusively to the underlying diseases.

items.title: Navigating Heart Transplantation in a Highly Sensitized Patient with Takayasu Arteritis: The Role of Perioperative Desensitization.
items.abstract: Introduction: Takayasu arteritis (TA) is a rare large-vessel vasculitis that in selected patients can lead to severe cardiovascular complications, including advanced heart failure (HF), requiring heart transplantation (HTx). Marked pre-transplant high levels of anti-HLA antibodies and notable sensitization substantially complicate donor selection and may prolong time spent on transplant waitlists. In highly sensitized recipients, HTx may therefore require individualized perioperative desensitization strategies to reduce the risk of antibody-mediated graft injury. Case Summary: We present the case of a 46-year-old woman with TA and advanced HF who underwent HTx after individualized perioperative desensitization in the setting of significant pre-transplant sensitization (PRA > 60%). Her postoperative course required intensive clinical and immunological monitoring and treatment. The early PT course was complicated by severe clinical deterioration, including a life-threatening episode of asystole that occurred in temporal association with peak anti-HLA class I and II antibody levels. Discussion: The case highlights the complexity of alloimmune management in a patient with TA and marked pre-transplant sensitization. Also, the temporal relationship between peak antibody levels and clinical instability suggests the need for close immune surveillance, tailored desensitization and individualized immunosuppressive treatment strategies in this high-risk group. Conclusions: This case describes the clinical course of a highly sensitized patient with TA who underwent HTx following an individualized perioperative desensitization strategy based on a modified Hannover protocol. Although transplantation was followed by substantial postoperative complications, the patient remained clinically stable during follow-up. The efficacy of the modified desensitization strategy cannot be established from a single case.

items.title: Salivary IFN-γ/IL-4 Ratio as a Mirror of Patient Experience: Unraveling Self-Reported Health and Disease Etiology in Sjögren's Disease-A Pilot Study.
items.abstract: Background/Objectives: To determine whether self-reports on the onset, perceived causes and activity of Sjögren's disease (SjD) can reflect the local immune status? Materials and methods: This prospective study enrolled a cohort of 80 patients with sicca symptoms (dry eyes and dry mouth) referred to the outpatient department of the State Research Institute Center for Innovative Medicine between September 2024 and January 2026. The study population comprised two distinct clinical groups: 37 patients diagnosed with SjD and 43 patients with non-autoimmune sicca syndrome (nonautoimmunSicca) due to gastroesophageal reflux disease (GERD). All patients indicated the perceived causes of their disease, the symptoms at the onset of the disease, and the activity of the disease using Visual analog scale (VAS). Cytokine levels in saliva were measured using enzyme-linked immunosorbent assay (ELISA). Results: The IFN-γ/IL-4 ratio was significantly increased in patients with SjD (median 158.7 (IQR 67.4-465.1) vs. 31.80 (IQR 20.9-45.5); p < 0.001). The IFN-γ/IL-4 ratio was significantly and negatively correlated with extraglandular symptoms at the onset of the disease, time from the 1st symptoms, salivary flow rates, and positively correlated with dryness score according to VAS in patients with SjD. The IFN-γ/IL-4 ratio was significantly and negatively associated with salivary flow rates and positively correlated with dryness score according to VAS in patients with nonautoimmunSicca. We also found a positive correlation between the perceived cause of the disease and the dryness score on the VAS, as well as a negative correlation between saliva flow rate and the concentration of IFN-γ in saliva among patients with SjD. The salivary IL-4 levels significantly and positively correlated with salivary flow rate, as well as negatively with pain and dryness score on the VAS in SjD group. Conclusions: Patient-reported information regarding disease onset, perceived causes, and symptoms severity of SjD significantly correlates with local Th1/Th2 mucosal immune status, suggesting that patient experiences may reflect underlying inflammatory trends and support patient-centered clinical evaluation.

items.title: Association of GSTM1 and GSTT1 Deletion Variants with Susceptibility to Behçet's Disease in a Saudi Population: A Case Control Study.
items.abstract: Behçet's disease (BD) is a chronic multisystem inflammatory disorder in which genetic susceptibility and oxidative stress may contribute to disease pathogenesis. Glutathione S-transferase (GST) enzymes play an important role in cellular antioxidant defense. Deletion variants of the GSTM1 and GSTT1 result in loss of enzyme activity and may influence susceptibility to BD. A case control study was conducted including 79 patients with BD ( n = 79) and 100 controls ( n = 100) from Saudi Arabia. Genotyping of GSTM1 and GSTT1 deletion variants was performed using multiplex polymerase chain reaction. Genotype frequencies were compared using odds ratios (ORs) and 95% confidence intervals (CIs). The frequency of GSTM1 - null genotype was significantly more frequent in BD cases than in controls (OR = 2.11, 95% CI = 1.15-3.85; p = 0.016; adjusted OR = 2.51, 95% CI = 1.24-5.07; p = 0.010; corrected p = 0.021). The GSTT1 - null genotype was also more frequent (OR = 3.10, 95% CI = 1.63-5.89; p = 0.001; adjusted OR = 2.25, 95% CI = 1.08-4.68; p = 0.030), although this association did not remain significant after Bonferroni correction (corrected p = 0.060). Combined genotype analysis showed a significant association for GSTM1 -/ GSTT1 - (OR = 6.90, 95% CI = 2.65-17.98; p < 0.001; adjusted OR = 6.35, 95% CI = 1.89-21.35; p = 0.003) compared with the GSTM1 +/ GSTT1 + genotype, which remained significant after Bonferroni correction (corrected p = 0.008). Stratified analyses did not demonstrate a clear association between GST deletion variants and disease activity or gender. The present study suggests that the GSTM1 - genotype and the combined GSTM1 -/ GSTT1 - genotype are significantly associated with susceptibility to BD in the Saudi population, independent of age and sex.

items.title: Integrated Transcriptomic Analysis Identifies a Ferroptosis-Related Gene Signature Underlying Macrophage Heterogeneity and Immune Dysregulation in Rheumatoid Arthritis Synovium.
items.abstract: Ferroptosis contributes to rheumatoid arthritis (RA), but the key regulators and their cell-specific functions in the synovial microenvironment remain incompletely understood. This study aimed to identify robust ferroptosis-associated biomarkers and define their cellular context through an integrated transcriptomic framework. Bulk synovial transcriptomic datasets were integrated using differential expression, weighted gene co-expression network analysis, and a curated ferroptosis gene set. Candidate genes were prioritized using three feature-selection algorithms and validated across twelve models. Immune infiltration, single-cell RNA sequencing, pseudotime, CellChat, and virtual gene perturbation analyses characterized their cellular and functional context. Six ferroptosis-related genes ( AIM2 , HCP5 , CAPG , ALOX5 , TYMS , and RUNX3 ) formed a diagnostic signature discriminating RA from healthy synovium (mean leakage-free test AUC 0.977 across five training-only re-derivations; 0.9375 in the primary split), with consistent leave-one-dataset-out and osteoarthritis-control validation. These genes linked to adaptive immune and ferroptosis-associated transcriptional programs. Single-cell analysis localized this transcriptional score to macrophages, where ferroptosis-signature-high macrophages occupied a central communication-network position and showed collagen-pathway enrichment; because RA and healthy samples were not fully independent of dataset origin, this finding is hypothesis-generating. Pseudotime analysis suggested progressive induction of these genes toward an inflammatory NF-κB/TNF/IL-17 terminal state, and virtual perturbation suggested convergence on mitochondrial oxidative phosphorylation networks that persisted after removing sex-chromosome genes, though residual sex-associated effects cannot be fully excluded. This study identifies a biologically interpretable ferroptosis-related gene signature and suggests ferroptosis-associated macrophage reprogramming may contribute to immune dysregulation in RA synovium. The single-cell findings are hypothesis-generating given the cohort design, while the diagnostic signature was supported by leakage-free, cross-cohort, and disease-specificity analyses, providing candidate biomarkers and therapeutic targets for RA.

items.title: Cellular Metabolic Heterogeneity and Therapeutic Targeting in Rheumatoid Arthritis.
items.abstract: Metabolic abnormalities in rheumatoid arthritis (RA) differ across cell populations and anatomical compartments. Glycolytic synovial fibroblasts coexist with blood T-cell populations showing impaired glycolytic induction or mitochondrial function, while macrophage metabolism can sustain inflammation or tissue protection. These differences complicate systemic metabolic inhibition. This narrative review integrates human RA studies, experimental arthritis and mechanistic work in other systems to identify dependencies that support defined pathogenic functions. We examine metabolite transport, nutrient adaptation and nutrient and energy sensing, distinguishing causal perturbation from descriptive signatures and preclinical hypotheses from clinical efficacy signals. Systemic cardiometabolic disease and nutritional interventions provide a clinical context for interpreting local metabolic findings. Small trials of repurposed drugs suggest possible benefit during treatment, but do not establish durable metabolic correction. We propose that a claim of reprogramming requires persistent functional change after drug removal, exclusion of residual exposure and selective cell loss, and preservation of immune regulation and host defence. These criteria could guide more selective metabolic interventions and their evaluation in patient tissue.

items.title: The Antisynthetase Syndrome: A Review.
items.abstract: Anti-synthetase syndrome (ASyS) is a relatively new and distinct clinical entity within the group of idiopathic inflammatory myopathies (IIM) characterized by the presence of autoantibodies targeting aminoacyl-tRNA synthetase (ARS), a family of enzymes responsible for protein translation but now recognized to possess important extracellular immunomodulatory functions. Anti-Jo-1 remains the most prevalent and studied antibody, but there exist additional antibodies, including PL-7, PL-12, EJ, OJ, KS, Zo, and Ha. These antibodies define a clinically similar but heterogenic syndrome with a variable combination of inflammatory myopathy, interstitial lung disease (ILD), inflammatory arthritis, and Raynaud's phenomenon. Only a minority of patients initially present with multiple symptoms, whereas isolated pulmonary, muscle, or articular manifestations frequently predominate. Interstitial lung disease remains the predominant cause of morbidity and mortality, but neuromuscular involvement is central to disease pathogenesis and patient disability. Current evidence supports a concept of pathogenesis in which genetically susceptible individuals develop aberrant innate and adaptive immune responses from tissue injury, leading to persistent inflammation and progressive fibrosis. Despite advances in understanding ASyS, the disease remains associated with significant morbidity and mortality, largely driven by ILD. This review summarizes current evidence regarding pathogenesis, genetic susceptibility, clinical manifestations, diagnostic evaluation, and evolving treatment strategies for ASyS.

items.title: Quadruple-negative autoantibody status and interstitial lung disease progression in systemic sclerosis.
items.abstract: To evaluate the association between disease-specific autoantibody profiles and disease progression in systemic sclerosis-associated interstitial lung disease (SSc-ILD), with a focus on a quadruple-negative phenotype. This retrospective cohort study included 80 patients with SSc-ILD who were followed for at least 12 months at a single tertiary centre. ILD progression was defined according to the OMERACT criteria and/or worsening on high-resolution computed tomography. Autoantibody status was categorized based on four antibodies: anti-topoisomerase I, anti-centromere, anti-RNA polymerase III and anti-U1-RNP. Quadruple-negative (QN) was defined as negativity for all four antibodies. Factors associated with ILD progression were evaluated using multivariable logistic regression. Exploratory comprehensive autoantibody profiling was performed in patients with available stored serum samples. During a median follow-up of 44.5 months, disease progression occurred in 32 of 80 patients with SSc-ILD. Anti-centromere antibody (ACA) positivity was associated with a lower risk of progression, whereas anti-topoisomerase I antibody positivity was not associated with disease progression (Model 2: OR 3.19, 95% CI 0.70-14.60). Compared with ACA positivity, QN status was associated with ILD progression (Model 2: OR 10.40, 95% confidence interval [CI] 1.77-60.70). However, CIs were wide. Exploratory analyses showed a high prevalence of anti-Ro-52 antibody positivity among patients with QN status. QN autoantibody status may be associated with an increased risk of ILD progression in SSc. The QN status may represent a heterogeneous serological category that could help identify patients who require closer clinical monitoring. However, these results are hypothesis-generating and require validation in larger, independent cohorts.

items.title: Baseline Disease Activity and Moderate-to-High Disease Activity at 6 Months in Rheumatoid Arthritis-Associated Interstitial Lung Disease: A Multicentre Real-World Study from the ANSWER Cohort.
items.abstract: Background/Objectives : In rheumatoid arthritis-associated interstitial lung disease (RA-ILD), factors associated with moderate-to-high disease activity (MDA/HDA) during follow-up are not well defined. We examined baseline factors associated with MDA/HDA at 6 months. Methods : We analyzed 278 patients with RA-ILD from the multicentre ANSWER cohort. At 6 months, patients were classified by the 28-joint Disease Activity Score using erythrocyte sedimentation rate (DAS28-ESR) as remission/low disease activity (LDA) or MDA/HDA. Logistic regression used age and baseline DAS28-ESR as continuous variables ( n = 178 with complete baseline DAS28-ESR); discrimination, calibration and optimism (1000 bootstrap resamples) were assessed. A sensitivity analysis used the ESR-free Clinical Disease Activity Index (CDAI) as the outcome. Results : In all, 148 patients achieved remission/LDA and 130 had MDA/HDA. Baseline DAS28-ESR was independently associated with MDA/HDA (odds ratio 2.01 per point, 95% CI 1.57-2.57), as was age (1.05 per year, 1.01-1.08). The area under the curve was 0.768 for DAS28-ESR alone and 0.776 with age added; internal validation of the two-variable model showed little estimated optimism (corrected area 0.772, calibration slope 0.984, 95% CI 0.693-1.396). With the CDAI-based outcome, the association with age was not reproduced (odds ratio 1.00, 0.97-1.04). Conclusions : Baseline disease activity is strongly associated with MDA/HDA at 6 months in RA-ILD. The incremental value of age was small, and the association with age was not reproduced when the outcome was defined by the CDAI. The age finding should therefore be regarded as secondary and dependent on the disease activity measure used. External and prospective validation is required before these findings are applied clinically.

items.title: Rheumatoid Arthritis, Serologic Status and Risk of Heart Failure: A National Cohort Study.
items.abstract: A limited number of studies have explored the association between rheumatoid arthritis (RA) and heart failure (HF) based on HF subtype (ischemic and non-ischemic) and RA serostatus. This study aimed to examine the association between RA and incident HF, considering serostatus (seropositive RA[SPRA], seronegative RA[SNRA]) and HF subtype. This retrospective cohort utilized nationwide population data from the National Health Insurance Service (NHIS) of Korea. The study analyzed 46,975 RA patients (33,424 SPRA, 13,551 SNRA) diagnosed in 2010-2017, along with 140,925 matched non-RA controls. The RA patients had a higher risk of overall HF (adjusted hazard ratio (aHR) 1.97, 95% confidence interval (CI) 1.68-2.32), and risk was more prominent for ischemic HF (aHR 2.24, 95% CI 1.86-2.71) than non-ischemic HF (aHR 1.36, 95% CI 0.97-1.90). Compared with controls, the risk of overall HF was increased in both SPRA (aHR 2.13, 95% CI 1.78-2.55) and SNRA (aHR 1.59, 95% CI 1.19-2.11), with a non-significant trend toward a higher risk in SPRA than in SNRA (aHR 1.35, 95% CI 0.99-1.83). For non-ischemic HF, the risk was increased in SPRA (aHR 1.60, 95% CI 1.12-2.28) but not in SNRA (aHR 0.71, 95% CI 0.32-1.51); however, this finding was based on a small number of events. This study demonstrates that RA was significantly associated with an increased risk of overall and ischemic HF, with a non-significant trend toward an increased risk of non-ischemic HF. The increased risk of ischemic HF was observed in both SPRA and SNRA, whereas the difference in non-ischemic HF risk by serostatus should be interpreted with caution due to the small number of events.

items.title: Association between intake of different beverages and risk of hyperuricemia and gout: a risk factor and dose-response meta-analysis.
items.abstract: The purpose of this study is to thoroughly review and compile evidence regarding the relationship between the consumption of various drinks and the risk of developing gout and hyperuricemia (HUA). We conducted a comprehensive search of PubMed, Embase, the Cochrane Library, and Web of Science to find cross-sectional, cohort, and case-control studies examining the link between the consumption of various beverages and HUA or gout. Fixed-effects models and random-effects models were used for the meta-analysis. Stata 18.0 was employed for meta-analysis and dose-response analysis to determine pooled odds ratios (ORs) and hazard ratios (HRs) with 95% confidence intervals (CIs). Statistical heterogeneity was quantified using the I 2 statistic. Sensitivity analyses were performed using the leave-one-out method. Publication bias was assessed by funnel plot inspection and Egger's test. The study included a total of 52 articles. The meta-analysis showed that alcohol intake (OR = 1.809, 95% CI: 1.372-2.385, p  < 0.001 for gout; OR = 1.524, 95% CI: 1.363-1.703, p  < 0.001 for HUA) and intake of sugar-sweetened beverages (SSBs) (OR = 1.371, 95% CI: 1.059-1.776, p  = 0.017 for gout; OR = 1.478, 95% CI: 1.342-1.627, p  < 0.001 for HUA) were connected to an elevated risk of gout and HUA, and at conventional intake levels, tea was associated with an increased risk of HUA among female (OR = 1.294, 95% CI: 1.081-1.549, p  = 0.005) subgroups. Coffee intake was linked to a reduced risk of developing gout (OR = 0.543, 95% CI: 0.341-0.866, p  = 0.010). Analyses of dose-response revealed a negative correlation between coffee consumption and gout, while alcohol and sugar-sweetened beverages were positively linked to both gout and hyperuricemia. Nonlinear relationships were found between alcohol consumption and gout, as well as between sugar-sweetened beverage consumption and hyperuricemia, but not for the other overall associations. These results were exploratory due to the limited number of studies included in each analysis. Substantial between-study heterogeneity was observed across most analyses, reflecting variation in study design, population characteristics, and exposure definitions. Leave-one-out sensitivity analyses typically indicated consistent association directions, but the statistical significance was affected by which studies were included for certain outcomes. Given the relatively small number of studies included in most analyses, Egger's test may have had insufficient statistical power to reliably detect funnel plot asymmetry. The publication bias assessments reported here are therefore exploratory in nature, and the possibility of small-study effects or selective reporting cannot be fully excluded. Alcohol and SSB intake were associated with higher odds of gout and HUA. Current research indicates that there is an association between coffee intake and a reduced risk of gout, while tea consumption may be associated with an increased risk of HUA in female subgroups, though this requires further validation. https://www.crd.york.ac.uk/prospero/, identifier CRD420261279131.

items.title: Clinical Factors and Cumulative Smoking Burden Associated with Anti-TNF Switching in Radiographic Axial Spondyloarthritis: A Real-World Cohort Study.
items.abstract: Background/Objectives: Anti-tumor necrosis factor (anti-TNF) switching remains common in radiographic axial spondyloarthritis (r-axSpA). We aimed to evaluate cumulative smoking burden and clinical factors associated with anti-TNF switching. Methods: This retrospective single-center cohort included 212 patients with r-axSpA. Clinical data were collected from medical records. Bivariate comparisons, Kaplan-Meier analysis and multivariable Cox regression assessed switching, with a cause-specific sensitivity analysis for lack-of-response switching. Results: Eighty patients (37.7%) switched initial anti-TNF agent, including 70 (87.5%) for lack of response. While the global comparison of smoking status was nonsignificant ( p = 0.105), exploratory unadjusted comparisons of current smokers versus former and never-smokers combined showed associations with all-cause ( p = 0.035) and lack-of-response switching ( p = 0.012). In adjusted Cox analysis, cumulative smoking burden was associated with increased switching hazard (HR 1.025 per pack-year, 95% CI 1.011-1.039; p < 0.001), alongside peripheral articular involvement (HR: 2.0, 95% CI 1.216-3.296, p = 0.006), higher BASDAI at anti-TNF initiation (HR: 1.02, 95% CI 1.004-1.029, p = 0.007) and later calendar year of treatment initiation (HR: 1.24, 95% CI 1.107-1.394, p < 0.001). Smoking burden >20 pack-years was associated with a higher adjusted switching hazard compared with never-smokers (HR 3.54, 95% CI 2.081-6.033; p < 0.001). Among ever-smokers, Kaplan-Meier comparisons showed shorter drug survival with >20 versus ≤10 and >10-20 pack-years (both p < 0.001). Conclusions: Cumulative smoking burden was associated with an increased hazard of anti-TNF switching, particularly among patients with >20 pack-years. Quantifying smoking exposure may provide additional information beyond smoking status alone.

items.title: Cross-Cultural Adaptation and Psychometric Evaluation of the Italian Version of the Systemic Lupus Erythematosus Symptom Checklist.
items.abstract: Background/Objectives : Systemic lupus erythematosus (SLE) causes a wide, fluctuating range of disease- and treatment-related symptoms that objective indices capture only partially. The SLE Symptom Checklist (SSC) is a disease-specific patient-reported measure of symptom occurrence and perceived burden, but no Italian version exists, and its latent structure has never been examined with confirmatory methods. This study aimed to translate, culturally adapt and psychometrically evaluate the Italian SSC in patients with SLE, and to characterize its dimensionality. Methods : A cross-sectional study was conducted in 331 patients (301 with SLE, with or without antiphospholipid syndrome [APS]; 30 with primary APS as an exploratory subgroup). Items were recoded to a single 0-4 ordinal metric (0 = absent; 1-4 = burden). Analyses included exploratory factor analysis of polychoric correlations, within-sample ordinal confirmatory factor analysis, cross-validation, bifactor modeling and a sensitivity analysis excluding primary APS. Concurrent validity was assessed against the EQ-5D visual analog scale (EQ-VAS), GAD-7 and PHQ-9. Results : An exploratory 23-item short form, derived with loading-based retention rules, comprised five symptom clusters (pain/somatic-systemic, neuropsychological/mood, skin/treatment-related, appetite/weight, photosensitivity) and showed acceptable within-sample fit (CFI = 0.96; RMSEA = 0.055), but limited discriminant validity. Bifactor analysis showed a dominant general factor (ECV = 0.61; omega hierarchical = 0.85). The 38-item total score showed high internal consistency (α = 0.92) and correlated with EQ-VAS (ρ = -0.49), GAD-7 (ρ = 0.41) and PHQ-9 (ρ = 0.57); results were similar after excluding primary APS. Conclusions : The Italian SSC showed good internal consistency, content validity and concurrent validity, and should be considered an essentially unidimensional measure of symptom burden with five descriptive symptom clusters requiring independent confirmation. Its usefulness for longitudinal monitoring remains to be established.

items.title: Benefits and Complications of Long-Term Low-Dose Glucocorticoids in Rheumatoid Arthritis: A Traditional Review.
items.abstract: Long-term low-dose glucocorticoid therapy remains widely used in rheumatoid arthritis (RA), despite concerns regarding cumulative toxicity. This traditional review evaluates the clinical benefits and complications of oral glucocorticoids at doses of ≤7.5 mg/day prednisone equivalent in adults with RA, with particular attention to disease control, bone health, cardiovascular outcomes, infection, and glucocorticoid withdrawal. A literature search of PubMed Advanced, PubMed Central, and Google Scholar conducted from July 1 to October 9, 2026, identified 56 potentially relevant studies, of which 36 were selected for qualitative synthesis. Evidence from randomized controlled trials, observational cohorts, systematic reviews, meta-analyses, and clinical guidelines was evaluated. Low-dose glucocorticoids provide measurable clinical benefits, including reduced disease activity, prevention of disease flares, and slowing of radiographic joint damage. However, these benefits must be balanced against cumulative adverse effects. Infection was the most consistently demonstrated complication, with observational evidence showing an increased risk even at doses of ≤5 mg/day. Evidence regarding skeletal toxicity was mixed: observational studies associated low-dose glucocorticoids with reduced bone mineral density (BMD) and increased fracture risk, whereas randomized trial data suggested less pronounced effects when inflammation was controlled and bone-protective therapy was used. Cardiovascular risk also remained uncertain at very low doses and was influenced by baseline cardiovascular risk and cumulative exposure. Early initiation of effective biologic or targeted synthetic disease-modifying antirheumatic drugs (DMARDs) was associated with greater success in glucocorticoid discontinuation, while tapering could increase the risk of disease flare in patients with established low disease activity. Overall, low-dose glucocorticoids retain clinically meaningful efficacy in RA, but long-term use is associated with important cumulative risks, particularly infection. When continued therapy is necessary, the minimum effective dose should be used with regular reassessment and appropriate monitoring and preventive measures. When disease control permits, gradual tapering and steroid-sparing therapy should be prioritized.

items.title: Multiplex complement profiling uncovers complement activation signatures in microvascular manifestations of antiphospholipid syndrome.
items.abstract: The 2023 American College of Rheumatology/European League Against Rheumatism antiphospholipid syndrome (APS) classification criteria define a clinical domain characterized mainly by microvascular thrombosis formation and is associated with complement activation. We aimed to evaluate the relationship between the complement profile and organ-specific manifestations of APS, especially microvascular APS (MAPS). Patients who fulfilled the 2023 ACR/EULAR APS classification criteria were enrolled. Plasma levels of complement components (Ba, Bb, C3a, C4a, C5a, soluble C5b-9, factor H, factor I, C1q, C2, C3, C4, C5, factor D, and factor P) were quantified by chemiluminescent multiplex enzyme-linked immunosorbent assays. Cluster analysis was performed to identify distinct complement activation profiles among clinical subgroups. A total of 58 patients with APS, including 51 patients with MAPS consecutively enrolled between August 2023 and June 2025, and 20 healthy controls (HCs) were included in the study. Compared with HCs, patients with MAPS had significantly higher plasma levels of Ba, C3a, C4a, and sC5b-9, and significantly lower levels of C1q, C2, and factor P (all P < .05). Cluster analysis identified 3 subgroups: cluster 1 characterized by predominant MAPS manifestations with marked alternative pathway activation; cluster 2 enriched for myocardial disease and antinuclear antibody positivity, showing predominance of classical and lectin pathway activation; and cluster 3 characterized by macrovascular thrombosis with relatively mild complement activation. A predictive model combining factor P and C3a demonstrated good performance for MAPS (AUC = 0.898; sensitivity 82.4%; specificity 88.9%). Complement profiling may serve as a valuable tool for early identification of MAPS, disease monitoring, and guiding individualized treatment, highlighting the potential of complement-targeted therapies in MAPS.

items.title: Real-world trajectories in psoriatic arthritis under risankizumab therapy.
items.abstract: Risankizumab, a selective IL-23p19 inhibitor, has demonstrated efficacy in randomized clinical trials, but real-world data remain limited. To evaluate the real-world effectiveness and safety of risankizumab in PsA, and to identify baseline predictors of treatment response. This multicentre, retrospective, longitudinal, real-world study included 112 PsA patients fulfilling the CASPAR criteria enrolled across seven Italian combined dermato-rheumatology centers. DAPSA and other longitudinal variables were assessed at baseline, 3, 6, and 12 months. Patients were stratified as D2T (risankizumab as ≥3 rd -line biologic therapy) or nD2T, and as responders (DAPSA≤14) or non-responders at 6 months. Univariable and multivariable logistic regression analyses were performed to identify baseline predictors of DAPSA response. Risankizumab induced rapid and sustained improvement across PsA domains. A significant DAPSA reduction was observed (p<0.001), with 62.5% and 69% of evaluable patients achieving DAPSA response at 6 and 12 months, respectively. D2T patients exhibited higher baseline disease activity and burden but achieved comparable disease control by month 12. In multivariable analysis, higher baseline VAS pain was independently associated with lower odds of DAPSA response at 6 months (OR 0.74; 95% CI 0.55-0.96). Treatment persistence at 12 months was 82.1%. Adverse events were infrequent (4.5%), and only one led to treatment discontinuation. Risankizumab demonstrated real-world effectiveness and tolerability across heterogeneous PsA trajectories, including multi-failure patients. Higher baseline pain was independently associated with lower odds of achieving DAPSA remission/low disease activity, highlighting the importance of pain assessment in treatment stratification and supporting further studies on inflammatory and non-inflammatory determinants of response. Psoriatic arthritis is a long-term inflammatory disease that can affect the joints, skin and other parts of the body. Some people do not respond well to several treatments and can be difficult to treat. Risankizumab is a medicine that blocks part of the immune system involved in inflammation, but information on how it works in everyday clinical practice is still limited. In this study, we reviewed the medical records of 112 people with psoriatic arthritis treated with risankizumab in several Italian centres. We assessed disease activity before treatment and after 3, 6 and 12 months. We also compared patients who had already received several previous biologic treatments with those treated earlier in their disease course. Overall, risankizumab was associated with rapid and sustained improvement. Among patients with available data at 12 months, 69% reached remission or low disease activity. Patients who had already failed several previous biologic treatments had more severe disease at the start, but by 12 months their level of disease control was similar to that of other patients. We also found that patients reporting higher pain levels before starting risankizumab were less likely to reach good disease control after 6 months. This suggests that pain assessment may help doctors better understand which patients are most likely to benefit from treatment, and that both inflammatory and non-inflammatory causes of pain should be considered. Most patients continued risankizumab after 12 months. Side effects were uncommon, and only one patient stopped treatment because of an adverse event. Overall, these findings support risankizumab as an effective and well-tolerated option in real-world psoriatic arthritis care, including in patients with more complex treatment histories.

items.title: Novel machine learning models including adipose-muscle indices for the prediction of musculoskeletal complications in rheumatoid arthritis: A cross-sectional study.
items.abstract: This research aimed to investigate the associations of multiple adipose-muscle indices with secondary osteoporosis (OP) and sarcopenia in rheumatoid arthritis (RA) patients. To develop a comprehensive early diagnostic model for musculoskeletal loss in RA patients based on non-invasive adipose-muscle indices. A cross-sectional and Mendelian randomization (MR) study. Fourteen machine learning (ML) algorithms were applied to select features from 33 candidate variables and were incorporated to construct clinical predictive models for OP, sarcopenia, and osteo-sarcopenia (OS). Restricted cubic spline (RCS) analysis explored dose-response relationships. MR methods were used to analyze potential causal effects. Six key features were identified, of which the fat-to-muscle ratio (FMR) and the skeletal muscle mass-to-visceral fat area ratio (SVR) were the most prominent. FMR was a risk factor for OP, whereas SVR was a protective factor against sarcopenia. The LightGBM model demonstrated superior performance in predicting OS (AUC = 0.988). MR analysis further indicated that body fat mass fully mediated the causal pathway from RA to OP and sarcopenia. ML models based on hybrid adipose-muscle indices demonstrated exceptional predictive value for subclinical musculoskeletal loss in RA patients.
